Chapter 3 — Statistical Learning Theory

Why does a model that fits the training data also work on new data? When can we trust it, and how much?

3.1 Learning objectives¶

In Chapter 1 we trained models and measured them on data they had not seen. In Chapter 2 we learned that an average over a sample is an estimate of an expectation. This chapter puts the two ideas together. It answers a question that every method in the rest of the book silently relies on: why should a function that has a small error on the training set have a small error on future data? The answer is not “always”: we will see exactly when it holds, how fast it improves with the number of examples, and what it depends on.

After working through this chapter you will be able to:

  1. define the data distribution, the expected risk and the empirical risk, and explain why the whole of machine learning is about the gap between them;

  2. derive the Bayes-optimal predictor for the squared loss and for the 0–1 loss, and explain why a part of the error can never be removed;

  3. write empirical risk minimization (ERM) and split the excess risk into an approximation error and an estimation error;

  4. explain, with a short proof and with experiments, why the training error is optimistic, and quantify the optimism when many candidate models are compared;

  5. state Markov’s, Chebyshev’s and Hoeffding’s inequalities, and derive Hoeffding’s inequality;

  6. prove a generalization bound for a finite hypothesis class with the union bound, and turn it into a sample-complexity formula;

  7. define shattering, the growth function and the VC dimension, compute them for simple classes, and state the VC generalization bound;

  8. define the Rademacher complexity, derive its bound for norm-bounded linear classifiers, and explain why controlling the norm (regularization, large margins) controls generalization even when the dimension is larger than the number of examples;

  9. state the No Free Lunch theorem and explain what an inductive bias is;

  10. use Hoeffding’s inequality to size a test set, and judge honestly how loose the bounds of the theory are on a real data set.

Prerequisites. Chapters 1 and 2, in particular Sections 1.5 (loss and risk) and 2.6 (expectation, variance, the law of large numbers). Calculus and the matrix notation of the previous chapters. No measure theory: random variables are treated as in Chapter 2.

How to read this chapter. It is the most mathematical chapter of Part I, and it is built so that you can read it at two depths. Each section has the same rhythm: an idea in words, a precise statement, a proof (marked, and safe to skip at a first reading), and an experiment that makes the statement concrete. The experiments carry the message; the proofs explain why the message is true. If you skip every proof you will still be able to follow the book. If you read them all, you will have seen the three classical ways of measuring the capacity of a model: its size (Section 3.6), its shattering power (Section 3.7) and its ability to fit noise (Section 3.8).

A word about the data in this chapter

Theory talks about a distribution D\mathcal{D}D that is unknown in practice. To check a statement about D\mathcal{D}D numerically we need a world where we do know it. In Sections 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4 we therefore use a small simulated world, and from Section 3.6 on we also use a real data set (Breast Cancer, seen in Chapter 1), treated as the population from which we draw samples. Whenever a number comes from a simulation, the text says so.

3.2 The setting: distribution, loss, and risk¶

3.2.1 The data are random draws from an unknown distribution¶

Everything in this chapter rests on one modeling assumption. There is a joint distribution D\mathcal{D}D over pairs (x,y)(\mathbf{x}, y)(x,y) of an input and a label, which we cannot see, and the training set

S={(x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)}S = \{(\mathbf{x}_1, y_1), \dots, (\mathbf{x}_n, y_n)\}S={(x1​,y1​),…,(xn​,yn​)}
(1)

consists of nnn pairs drawn independently from D\mathcal{D}D (“i.i.d.”: independent and identically distributed). A future example, the one we care about, is one more independent draw from the same D\mathcal{D}D. A prediction function is a map fff from inputs to predictions y^=f(x)\hat y = f(\mathbf{x})y^​=f(x), and a loss ℓ(y,y^)≥0\ell(y, \hat y) \ge 0ℓ(y,y^​)≥0 scores a single prediction (Section 1.5). The two quantities that matter are

R(f)=E(x,y)∼D[ℓ(y,f(x))]andR^S(f)=1n∑i=1nℓ(yi,f(xi)).R(f) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x}, y) \sim \mathcal{D}}\big[\ell\big(y, f(\mathbf{x})\big)\big] \qquad\text{and}\qquad \hat{R}_S(f) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell\big(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i)\big).R(f)=E(x,y)∼D​[ℓ(y,f(x))]andR^S​(f)=n1​i=1∑n​ℓ(yi​,f(xi​)).
(2)

R(f)R(f)R(f) is the expected risk (also called the true risk or the generalization error): the average loss on a new example. R^S(f)\hat{R}_S(f)R^S​(f) is the empirical risk: the average loss on the training set, which we can compute. The first is what we want; the second is what we have. Section 2.6 told us that R^S(f)\hat{R}_S(f)R^S​(f) is a sample mean of the random variable ℓ(y,f(x))\ell(y, f(\mathbf{x}))ℓ(y,f(x)) and that R(f)R(f)R(f) is its expectation, so the whole chapter is about how far a sample mean can be from the mean when the function fff itself has been chosen by looking at the sample.

Pitfall — the i.i.d. assumption is a modeling choice, not a fact

The theory below applies when the training examples are independent draws and the future examples come from the same distribution. It fails, quietly, when the data are a time series (today resembles yesterday), when several rows come from the same patient or the same house (they are not independent), or when the model will be used on a different population from the one it was trained on. These situations do not make learning impossible, but the guarantees of this chapter no longer apply as stated, and the splitting strategy has to change (Chapter 5). Most “my model worked in the lab and failed in production” stories are violations of this assumption.

3.2.2 The best possible predictor: the Bayes predictor¶

If we knew D\mathcal{D}D, which function would we choose? Take the infimum of the risk over all functions,

R∗=inf⁡fR(f),R^\ast = \inf_{f} R(f),R∗=finf​R(f),
(3)

and call a function that achieves it a Bayes-optimal predictor f∗f^\astf∗. It is a benchmark that no method, however clever and however much data it has, can beat. It can be found one input at a time, because the risk is an average over x\mathbf{x}x of a conditional risk:

R(f)=Ex[ E[ℓ(y,f(x))∣x]⏟conditional risk at x ].R(f) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\Big[\,\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big[\ell(y, f(\mathbf{x})) \mid \mathbf{x}\big]}_{\text{conditional risk at } \mathbf{x}}\,\Big].R(f)=Ex​[conditional risk at xE[ℓ(y,f(x))∣x]​​].
(4)

This is the law of total expectation of Section 2.6. To make R(f)R(f)R(f) small it is enough, and necessary, to make the conditional risk small at every x\mathbf{x}x, which means choosing for each x\mathbf{x}x the best single prediction a=f(x)a = f(\mathbf{x})a=f(x) given what x\mathbf{x}x tells us about yyy. Let us do it for the two most common losses.

Squared loss (regression). Write η(x)=E[y∣x]\eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}]η(x)=E[y∣x], the conditional mean. For any number aaa,

E[(y−a)2∣x]=E[(y−η(x))2∣x]+(η(x)−a)2=Var⁡(y∣x)+(η(x)−a)2.\mathbb{E}\big[(y - a)^2 \mid \mathbf{x}\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[(y - \eta(\mathbf{x}))^2 \mid \mathbf{x}\big] + (\eta(\mathbf{x}) - a)^2 = \operatorname{Var}(y \mid \mathbf{x}) + (\eta(\mathbf{x}) - a)^2 .E[(y−a)2∣x]=E[(y−η(x))2∣x]+(η(x)−a)2=Var(y∣x)+(η(x)−a)2.
(5)

(Add and subtract η(x)\eta(\mathbf{x})η(x) inside the square; the cross term has zero expectation because E[y−η(x)∣x]=0\mathbb{E}[y - \eta(\mathbf{x}) \mid \mathbf{x}] = 0E[y−η(x)∣x]=0.) The second term is smallest, and equal to zero, for a=η(x)a = \eta(\mathbf{x})a=η(x). Hence

 f∗(x)=E[y∣x],R∗=E[Var⁡(y∣x)] andR(f)−R∗=E[(f(x)−η(x))2].\boxed{\,f^\ast(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}], \qquad R^\ast = \mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{Var}(y \mid \mathbf{x})\big]\,} \qquad\text{and}\qquad R(f) - R^\ast = \mathbb{E}\big[(f(\mathbf{x}) - \eta(\mathbf{x}))^2\big].f∗(x)=E[y∣x],R∗=E[Var(y∣x)]​andR(f)−R∗=E[(f(x)−η(x))2].
(6)

The best regression function is the conditional mean, and the floor R∗R^\astR∗ is the average noise around it: the part of yyy that the input does not determine. For a constant predictor (no input) this is the result of Section 1.5, the sample mean; for the Bayes predictor the same idea is applied at every x\mathbf{x}x.

0–1 loss (binary classification). Let y∈{0,1}y \in \{0, 1\}y∈{0,1} and η(x)=P(y=1∣x)\eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x})η(x)=P(y=1∣x). Predicting a∈{0,1}a \in \{0, 1\}a∈{0,1} is wrong with probability P(y≠a∣x)\mathbb{P}(y \neq a \mid \mathbf{x})P(y=a∣x), which is 1−η(x)1 - \eta(\mathbf{x})1−η(x) if a=1a = 1a=1 and η(x)\eta(\mathbf{x})η(x) if a=0a = 0a=0. The smaller of the two is obtained by predicting the more probable class:

 f∗(x)=I[η(x)>12],R∗=E[min⁡{η(x), 1−η(x)}] \boxed{\,f^\ast(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{I}\big[\eta(\mathbf{x}) > \tfrac12\big], \qquad R^\ast = \mathbb{E}\big[\min\{\eta(\mathbf{x}),\, 1 - \eta(\mathbf{x})\}\big]\,}f∗(x)=I[η(x)>21​],R∗=E[min{η(x),1−η(x)}]​
(7)

This is the Bayes classifier. By Bayes’ rule of Section 2.6 it can be written in terms of the class-conditional densities pk(x)p_k(\mathbf{x})pk​(x) and the priors πk=P(y=k)\pi_k = \mathbb{P}(y = k)πk​=P(y=k): predict class 1 when π1p1(x)>π0p0(x)\pi_1 p_1(\mathbf{x}) > \pi_0 p_0(\mathbf{x})π1​p1​(x)>π0​p0​(x). The floor R∗R^\astR∗ is the average, over x\mathbf{x}x, of the probability of the less likely class: it is zero only if the label is a deterministic function of the input.

(For the absolute loss ∣y−a∣\lvert y - a \rvert∣y−a∣ the same argument gives the conditional median instead of the mean; see Exercise 3.2.)

Key idea

Noise sets a floor. Even a perfect learner with infinite data has an error R∗>0R^\ast > 0R∗>0 whenever the label is not a function of the features alone. Two patients with identical measurements can have different outcomes; two e-mails with identical words can be spam and not spam. A model with 85% accuracy on a problem whose Bayes accuracy is 86% is excellent; the same model on a problem whose Bayes accuracy is 99% is poor. On real data R∗R^\astR∗ is unknown, which is why a single accuracy number can never tell whether there is room for improvement.

Worked example 3.1 — the Bayes classifier of two Gaussians¶

Let the input be a single number xxx and the two classes be equally likely, with x∣y=0∼N(0,1)x \mid y = 0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)x∣y=0∼N(0,1) and x∣y=1∼N(3,1)x \mid y = 1 \sim \mathcal{N}(3, 1)x∣y=1∼N(3,1). With equal priors the Bayes classifier predicts the class with the larger density; the two Gaussians have the same variance, so their densities are equal at the midpoint, and

f∗(x)=I[x>1.5].f^\ast(x) = \mathbb{I}[x > 1.5].f∗(x)=I[x>1.5].
(8)

An error occurs when a class-0 point falls to the right of 1.5 or a class-1 point falls to the left of it. By symmetry both events have the same probability, P(N(0,1)>1.5)=Φ(−1.5)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}(0, 1) > 1.5) = \Phi(-1.5)P(N(0,1)>1.5)=Φ(−1.5), where Φ\PhiΦ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard Gaussian. Hence

R∗=12 Φ(−1.5)+12 Φ(−1.5)=Φ(−1.5)≈0.0668.R^\ast = \tfrac12\,\Phi(-1.5) + \tfrac12\,\Phi(-1.5) = \Phi(-1.5) \approx 0.0668 .R∗=21​Φ(−1.5)+21​Φ(−1.5)=Φ(−1.5)≈0.0668.
(9)

Even in this friendly problem, 6.7% of the examples are misclassified by the best possible rule, because the two bells overlap. Let us check the number with a simulation.

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
n_mc = 1_000_000
y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=n_mc)                       # equally likely classes
x = rng.normal(loc=3.0 * y, scale=1.0)                  # class 0: N(0,1), class 1: N(3,1)

bayes_pred = (x > 1.5).astype(int)
print(f"exact Bayes risk  Phi(-1.5)      : {stats.norm.cdf(-1.5):.4f}")
print(f"Monte Carlo risk of the rule x>1.5: {np.mean(bayes_pred != y):.4f}")
for t in (1.0, 1.25, 1.75, 2.0):                        # any other threshold does worse
    print(f"risk of the rule x>{t:<4}          : {np.mean((x > t) != y):.4f}")

Monte Carlo risk of the rule x>1.5: 0.0668
risk of the rule x>1.0           : 0.0908
risk of the rule x>1.25          : 0.0730

3.2.3 A world where we know D\mathcal{D}D¶

For the experiments of this chapter we need a problem in the plane where the Bayes classifier is known, but where a linear classifier cannot reach it. Class 0 is a round Gaussian cloud centered at the origin. Class 1 is a narrow vertical band: a Gaussian with a small variance in x1x_1x1​ and a large variance in x2x_2x2​, centered at (0.6,0)(0.6, 0)(0.6,0). The classes are equally likely. We will call it the simulated world.

The log-ratio of two Gaussian densities is a quadratic function of x\mathbf{x}x, so the boundary of the Bayes classifier is a conic (here two curves), not a line. That is deliberate: it will let us see, in numbers, the difference between the best that any classifier can do and the best that a linear classifier can do.

from scipy.stats import multivariate_normal

# The simulated world: two classes in the plane, equally likely.
MU = [np.array([0.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.6, 0.0])]
COV = [np.diag([1.0, 1.0]), np.diag([0.1, 6.0])]
dens = [multivariate_normal(MU[k], COV[k]) for k in (0, 1)]


def sample_world(n, rng):
    """Draw n i.i.d. pairs (x, y) from the distribution D of the simulated world."""
    y = rng.integers(0, 2, size=n)
    X = np.empty((n, 2))
    for k in (0, 1):
        idx = y == k
        X[idx] = rng.multivariate_normal(MU[k], COV[k], size=idx.sum())
    return X, y


def bayes_predict(X):
    """The Bayes classifier: predict the class with the larger density (the priors are equal)."""
    return (dens[1].logpdf(X) > dens[0].logpdf(X)).astype(int)


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
X_big, y_big = sample_world(2_000_000, rng)
errors = bayes_predict(X_big) != y_big
R_BAYES = errors.mean()
print(f"Bayes risk R* of the simulated world: {R_BAYES:.4f}   (Monte Carlo error +/- {errors.std() / np.sqrt(len(errors)):.4f})")
print(f"error on class 0: {errors[y_big == 0].mean():.4f} | error on class 1: {errors[y_big == 1].mean():.4f}")
Bayes risk R* of the simulated world: 0.1891   (Monte Carlo error +/- 0.0003)
error on class 0: 0.2653 | error on class 1: 0.1128

About 19% of the points are misclassified by the best possible rule: the Bayes risk of this world is R∗≈0.189R^\ast \approx 0.189R∗≈0.189. The next cell finds the best linear classifier of this world by brute force (all directions, all thresholds, on 300,000 points) and measures its risk on points it has not seen. The search is cheap because a linear classifier in the plane is a direction and a threshold.

def best_linear_classifier(X, y, n_angles=360):
    """Exhaustive search of the linear classifier with the smallest 0-1 error: 'predict 1 if w.x > t'."""
    n, best = len(y), (1.0, None, None)
    for theta in np.linspace(0, np.pi, n_angles, endpoint=False):
        w = np.array([np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)])
        order = np.argsort(X @ w)
        ys, proj = y[order], (X @ w)[order]
        below1, below0 = np.cumsum(ys == 1), np.cumsum(ys == 0)
        err_pred1_above = below1 + (below0[-1] - below0)       # errors if we predict 1 above the cut after position i
        for sign, errs in ((1.0, err_pred1_above), (-1.0, n - err_pred1_above)):
            i = errs.argmin()
            if errs[i] / n < best[0]:
                cut = (proj[i] + proj[min(i + 1, n - 1)]) / 2
                best = (errs[i] / n, sign * w, sign * cut)
    return best


_, w_lin, t_lin = best_linear_classifier(X_big[:300_000], y_big[:300_000])
fresh = slice(300_000, None)                                      # points the search has never seen
R_LINEAR = np.mean((X_big[fresh] @ w_lin > t_lin).astype(int) != y_big[fresh])
print(f"best linear classifier: direction {np.round(w_lin, 3)}, threshold {t_lin:.3f}")
print(f"risk of the best linear classifier: {R_LINEAR:.4f}   (Bayes risk: {R_BAYES:.4f})")
best linear classifier: direction [1. 0.], threshold 0.117
risk of the best linear classifier: 0.2587   (Bayes risk: 0.1891)

The best linear classifier is a vertical line, with a risk of about 0.259: seven percentage points worse than the Bayes classifier, and no amount of data will close that gap, because the gap is a property of the class of functions, not of the sample. Figure 3.1 shows the two boundaries.

# Figure 3.1 — the simulated world: data, Bayes boundary, and the best linear boundary
def figure_3_1():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 7)
    X, y = sample_world(500, rng)

    gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3.6, 3.6, 400), np.linspace(-7.5, 7.5, 600))
    grid = np.column_stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()])
    log_ratio = (dens[1].logpdf(grid) - dens[0].logpdf(grid)).reshape(gx.shape)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 6.6))
    ax.scatter(*X[y == 0].T, s=16, color=BLUE, marker="o", alpha=0.75, label="class 0")
    ax.scatter(*X[y == 1].T, s=18, color=ORANGE, marker="^", alpha=0.85, label="class 1")
    ax.contour(gx, gy, log_ratio, levels=[0], colors=[VERMILION], linewidths=2.2)
    ax.plot([], [], color=VERMILION, linewidth=2.2, label=f"Bayes boundary (risk {R_BAYES:.3f})")
    ax.axvline(t_lin, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.8, label=f"best linear boundary (risk {R_LINEAR:.3f})")
    ax.set(xlabel="$x_1$", ylabel="$x_2$", xlim=(-3.6, 3.6), ylim=(-7.5, 7.5),
           title="The simulated world and its two boundaries")
    ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.11), ncol=2, frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_1()

Class 0 (circles) is the round cloud. Class 1 (triangles) is the tall thin band that crosses it. The Bayes boundary (solid) has two branches, and class 1 is predicted between them: a region that is narrow near the origin and widens for large ∣x2∣\lvert x_2 \rvert∣x2​∣, where the broad class-1 density wins over the round class-0 density. No single straight line can do that. The best line (dashed) simply cuts the cloud vertically near x1≈0.1x_1 \approx 0.1x1​≈0.1.

Try it

Change the covariance of class 1 in the cell that defines COV (for instance to np.diag([1.0, 1.0])) and re-run the notebook from that point on. With equal covariances the Bayes boundary becomes a straight line, the best linear classifier is the Bayes classifier, and the 7-point gap disappears.

3.3 Empirical risk minimization and the two sources of error¶

We cannot minimize R(f)R(f)R(f), because we do not know D\mathcal{D}D. We can minimize R^S(f)\hat{R}_S(f)R^S​(f), which we can compute, and we cannot afford to search over all functions: with a finite sample, some function always matches the training labels exactly (for instance, a table of the training set, which says nothing about new inputs). So we restrict the search to a hypothesis class H\mathcal{H}H, a set of functions chosen in advance: the lines in the plane, the polynomials of degree at most 3, the neural networks with a given architecture. Empirical risk minimization returns a function of H\mathcal{H}H with the smallest empirical risk:

f^S∈argmin⁡f∈HR^S(f).\hat f_S \in \operatorname*{argmin}_{f \in \mathcal{H}} \hat{R}_S(f).f^​S​∈f∈Hargmin​R^S​(f).
(10)

This is the principle announced in Section 1.5. Two remarks keep the story honest. First, f^S\hat f_Sf^​S​ depends on the random sample, so it is itself random: a different training set gives a different function. Second, for the 0–1 loss the minimization is computationally hard for many classes (minimizing the number of mistakes of a linear classifier is NP-hard in general), so practical methods minimize a smooth substitute such as the logistic loss (Chapter 6) or the hinge loss (Chapter 8). Here we think of ideal ERM, and in the experiments we use logistic regression as a practical stand-in.

3.3.1 The decomposition of the excess risk¶

Let fHf_{\mathcal{H}}fH​ be the best function in the class, fH∈argmin⁡f∈HR(f)f_{\mathcal{H}} \in \operatorname{argmin}_{f \in \mathcal{H}} R(f)fH​∈argminf∈H​R(f): the function we would pick if we knew D\mathcal{D}D but were limited to H\mathcal{H}H. Adding and subtracting R(fH)R(f_{\mathcal{H}})R(fH​) splits the excess risk of the learned function over the unbeatable Bayes risk into two parts:

R(f^S)−R∗⏟excess risk=[R(f^S)−R(fH)]⏟estimation error+[R(fH)−R∗]⏟approximation error.\underbrace{R(\hat f_S) - R^\ast}_{\text{excess risk}} = \underbrace{\big[R(\hat f_S) - R(f_{\mathcal{H}})\big]}_{\text{estimation error}} + \underbrace{\big[R(f_{\mathcal{H}}) - R^\ast\big]}_{\text{approximation error}} .excess riskR(f^​S​)−R∗​​=estimation error[R(f^​S​)−R(fH​)]​​+approximation error[R(fH​)−R∗]​​.
(11)

  • The approximation error measures how well the class can do even with perfect knowledge of D\mathcal{D}D. It does not depend on nnn or on the sample; it shrinks only if we enlarge H\mathcal{H}H. In the simulated world, the approximation error of the lines is 0.259−0.189=0.0700.259 - 0.189 = 0.0700.259−0.189=0.070.

  • The estimation error measures what we lose by choosing the function from a finite random sample instead of from D\mathcal{D}D. It is random, it shrinks as nnn grows, and it grows with the richness of H\mathcal{H}H (more candidates, more ways to be fooled by the sample, as Section 3.4 shows).

Figure 3.2 sketches the picture: the Bayes predictor lives outside the class, the best function in the class is the closest we can get, and ERM lands somewhere around it.

# Figure 3.2 — a schematic of the two sources of error (not to scale)
def figure_3_2():
    from matplotlib.patches import Ellipse

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 4.6))
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((5.0, 2.6), 9.6, 4.9, facecolor="#f2f2f2", edgecolor="gray", linewidth=1.5))
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((6.2, 2.35), 4.5, 2.7, facecolor=SKY, alpha=0.35, edgecolor=BLUE, linewidth=2))
    ax.text(0.9, 4.65, "all functions", fontsize=11, color="gray")
    ax.text(6.2, 3.3, r"hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$", fontsize=11, color=BLUE, ha="center")

    p_bayes, p_best, p_erm = (2.6, 2.3), (5.2, 2.2), (6.9, 1.65)
    ax.plot(*p_bayes, marker="*", markersize=16, color=VERMILION)
    ax.plot(*p_best, marker="o", markersize=9, color=BLUE)
    ax.plot(*p_erm, marker="s", markersize=9, color=ORANGE)
    ax.annotate(r"Bayes predictor $f^*$" "\n" r"risk $R^*$", p_bayes, xytext=(1.5, 0.85), fontsize=10.5, ha="center", color=VERMILION)
    ax.annotate(r"best in class $f_{\mathcal{H}}$", p_best, xytext=(4.7, 1.0), fontsize=10.5, ha="center", color=BLUE)
    ax.annotate(r"ERM solution $\hat f_S$", p_erm, xytext=(8.0, 0.75), fontsize=10.5, ha="center", color="#8a5a00")
    ax.annotate("", p_best, p_bayes, arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "<->", "color": "black", "linewidth": 1.6})
    ax.annotate("", p_erm, p_best, arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "<->", "color": "black", "linewidth": 1.6, "linestyle": "--"})
    ax.text(3.9, 2.62, "approximation\nerror", ha="center", fontsize=10)
    ax.text(6.35, 2.02, "estimation\nerror", ha="center", fontsize=10)
    ax.set(xlim=(0, 10), ylim=(0, 5.3))

figure_3_2()

3.3.2 The trade-off, measured¶

Enlarging H\mathcal{H}H reduces the approximation error and increases the estimation error. To see both effects we use classes of increasing richness: logistic regression on the polynomial features of degree mmm of (x1,x2)(x_1, x_2)(x1​,x2​), for m=1m = 1m=1 (lines), m=2m = 2m=2 (conics, which contain the Bayes classifier of this world, so the approximation error is zero), up to m=8m = 8m=8 (44 features). We draw many training sets of size nnn from the simulated world, fit each class, and measure the risk of the result on a fresh test set of 100,000 points, which gives the true risk up to a Monte Carlo error of about 0.001. We use a very weak regularization (C=1000) so that logistic regression behaves like unregularized ERM; the role of regularization is the subject of Chapter 6.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler


def make_poly_model(degree):
    return make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False), StandardScaler(),
                         LogisticRegression(C=1000.0, max_iter=5000))


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 1)
X_test, y_test = sample_world(100_000, rng)          # one big test set: its error is the true risk, up to ~0.001


def risks(degree, n, reps):
    """Mean training error and mean true risk of the fitted model, over `reps` training sets of size n."""
    train_err, test_err = [], []
    for _ in range(reps):
        X, y = sample_world(n, rng)
        model = make_poly_model(degree).fit(X, y)
        train_err.append(np.mean(model.predict(X) != y))
        test_err.append(np.mean(model.predict(X_test) != y_test))
    return np.mean(train_err), np.mean(test_err)


degrees = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8]
sizes_left = [30, 300, 3000]
by_degree = {n: [risks(m, n, reps=60) for m in degrees] for n in sizes_left}

table = pd.DataFrame({f"n={n}, test risk": [r[1] for r in by_degree[n]] for n in sizes_left}, index=degrees)
table["n=30, TRAINING error"] = [r[0] for r in by_degree[30]]
table.index.name = "degree m"
print(f"Bayes risk R* = {R_BAYES:.3f}; best linear classifier = {R_LINEAR:.3f}")
table.round(3)
Bayes risk R* = 0.189; best linear classifier = 0.259
Loading...

Read the table column by column.

  • n=30n = 30n=30 (few data). The test risk is U-shaped: it falls from 0.34 (lines, large approximation error) to its minimum of 0.25 at degree 2, and then rises again to 0.30 at degree 8, because a class with 44 features has too much freedom for 30 points: the estimation error dominates. The training error (last column) does the opposite: it decreases all the way down to 0.05. The training error always prefers the richer class, and is therefore useless for choosing it.

  • n=300n = 300n=300. The best class is still degree 2, and the penalty for the richer classes has shrunk (0.207 at degree 8): more data, smaller estimation error.

  • n=3000n = 3000n=3000. Every class with degree ≥2\ge 2≥2 is within noise of the Bayes risk (0.189): the estimation error has become negligible, and what separates the classes is only the approximation error, which is zero for all of them. The lines, instead, stay at 0.28 (the logistic loss is a proxy for the 0–1 loss, so it does a little worse than the best line, 0.259).

The second experiment shows the effect of nnn for three classes, in a learning curve.

sizes_curve = [10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640, 1280, 2560]
curve_degrees = [1, 2, 8]
curves = {m: [risks(m, n, reps=100 if n <= 320 else 40) for n in sizes_curve] for m in curve_degrees}
pd.DataFrame({f"degree {m}": [r[1] for r in curves[m]] for m in curve_degrees}, index=pd.Index(sizes_curve, name="n")).round(3)
Loading...
# Figure 3.3 — approximation vs estimation error, measured in the simulated world
def figure_3_3():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.4))

    ax = axes[0]
    styles = {30: (VERMILION, "o", "-"), 300: (BLUE, "s", "--"), 3000: (GREEN, "^", ":")}
    for n in sizes_left:
        color, marker, ls = styles[n]
        ax.plot(degrees, [r[1] for r in by_degree[n]], marker=marker, linestyle=ls, color=color, linewidth=2, label=f"test risk, n = {n}")
    ax.plot(degrees, [r[0] for r in by_degree[30]], marker="o", linestyle="-", color=VERMILION, alpha=0.4, label="training error, n = 30")
    ax.axhline(R_BAYES, color="black", linewidth=1.2)
    ax.text(8.1, R_BAYES - 0.012, "Bayes risk", ha="right", va="top", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.set(xlabel="degree $m$ of the polynomial features (richness of $\\mathcal{H}$)", ylabel="0-1 risk",
           title="(a) risk against richness, at fixed $n$")
    ax.set_ylim(0.03, 0.47)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, ncol=2, loc="upper right")

    ax = axes[1]
    styles = {1: (VERMILION, "o", "-"), 2: (BLUE, "s", "--"), 8: (GREEN, "^", ":")}
    names = {1: "degree 1 (lines)", 2: "degree 2 (contains the Bayes classifier)", 8: "degree 8 (44 features)"}
    for m in curve_degrees:

    ax.axhline(R_BAYES, color="black", linewidth=1.2)
    ax.axhline(R_LINEAR, color="gray", linewidth=1.2, linestyle="--")
    ax.text(10.5, R_BAYES + 0.004, "Bayes risk", va="bottom", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.text(2600, R_LINEAR + 0.004, "best line", va="bottom", ha="right", fontsize=9.5, color="gray")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="training-set size $n$", ylabel="true risk", title="(b) learning curves")

figure_3_3()

Panel (b) is the picture to remember. The lines (vermilion) flatten out high above the Bayes risk: more data will never help, because the approximation error is there to stay. Degree 2 (blue) converges to the Bayes risk quickly, since its class contains the Bayes classifier and has only 5 features. Degree 8 (green) also converges to the Bayes risk, since it contains degree 2, but it needs about four times more data to get there (it reaches a risk of 0.20 at n=320n = 320n=320, where degree 2 had it at n=80n = 80n=80): its extra freedom is a liability when nnn is small.

Key idea

The right complexity depends on the amount of data. With n=30n = 30n=30 the best class is small even if it is “wrong”; with n=3000n = 3000n=3000 any sufficiently rich class works. A fixed choice of model family is a bet on the amount of data and on the structure of the problem. The rest of Part II is about methods that adapt their complexity to the data: regularization (Chapter 6), margins (Chapter 8), pruning and ensembles (Chapter 11), and about choosing it by validation (Chapter 5), since the training error cannot do it, as the table has just shown. For the squared loss the same decomposition has a famous name, the bias–variance trade-off, studied in Chapter 4.

3.4 Why the training error is optimistic¶

Why does the training error of the richer classes keep falling while the test risk rises? There are two different statements to prove, and the difference between them is the heart of this chapter.

For a fixed function, the empirical risk is an honest estimate. Suppose fff was chosen before seeing SSS (by a colleague, by a previous data set, by a coin). Then ℓ(yi,f(xi))\ell(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i))ℓ(yi​,f(xi​)) are i.i.d. random variables with mean R(f)R(f)R(f), and by the linearity of expectation

ES[R^S(f)]=1n∑i=1nE[ℓ(yi,f(xi))]=R(f).\mathbb{E}_S\big[\hat{R}_S(f)\big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\big[\ell(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i))\big] = R(f).ES​[R^S​(f)]=n1​i=1∑n​E[ℓ(yi​,f(xi​))]=R(f).
(12)

The empirical risk is an unbiased estimate of the true risk, and the law of large numbers (Section 2.6.6) says that it converges to it as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞. This is why a test set, used once on one function, can be trusted (Section 3.10).

For the function chosen by ERM it is not. The function f^S\hat f_Sf^​S​ is selected because it has a small empirical risk on this particular SSS. Using only the definition of ERM, R^S(f^S)≤R^S(fH)\hat{R}_S(\hat f_S) \le \hat{R}_S(f_{\mathcal{H}})R^S​(f^​S​)≤R^S​(fH​) for the best function in the class, and fHf_{\mathcal{H}}fH​ is a fixed function (it does not depend on SSS), so the previous paragraph applies to it:

ES[R^S(f^S)]  ≤  ES[R^S(fH)]  =  R(fH)  ≤  ES[R(f^S)].\mathbb{E}_S\big[\hat{R}_S(\hat f_S)\big] \;\le\; \mathbb{E}_S\big[\hat{R}_S(f_{\mathcal{H}})\big] \;=\; R(f_{\mathcal{H}}) \;\le\; \mathbb{E}_S\big[R(\hat f_S)\big].ES​[R^S​(f^​S​)]≤ES​[R^S​(fH​)]=R(fH​)≤ES​[R(f^​S​)].
(13)

The last inequality holds because R(fH)R(f_{\mathcal{H}})R(fH​) is the smallest risk in the class and f^S\hat f_Sf^​S​ belongs to the class. In words, on average, the training error of the ERM solution is below the best achievable risk in the class, which is below the true risk of the ERM solution. The training error is a biased, over-optimistic estimate, and the optimism is larger when the class is richer, as the table of Section 3.3 showed.

3.4.1 Optimism grows with the number of candidates¶

How large can the optimism be? Take the most extreme situation: the labels are pure coin flips, so that every function has true risk exactly 12\tfrac1221​ and nothing can be learned. We try mmm candidate functions, so that each one predicts the nnn training labels at random and independently of the others (for instance, mmm random models, or mmm random subsets of features). The training error of each candidate is Binomial(n,12)/n\text{Binomial}(n, \tfrac12)/nBinomial(n,21​)/n, and ERM keeps the smallest of the mmm values. Its expectation is computed exactly from the cumulative distribution of the binomial: since the minimum of mmm independent variables exceeds k−1k - 1k−1 with probability (P(Bin≥k))m\big(\mathbb{P}(\text{Bin} \ge k)\big)^m(P(Bin≥k))m,

E[min⁡j≤mR^j]=1n∑k=1n(1−F(k−1))m,F=cdf of Binomial(n,12).\mathbb{E}\Big[\min_{j \le m} \hat{R}_j\Big] = \frac1n \sum_{k=1}^{n} \big(1 - F(k-1)\big)^{m}, \qquad F = \text{cdf of } \text{Binomial}(n, \tfrac12).E[j≤mmin​R^j​]=n1​k=1∑n​(1−F(k−1))m,F=cdf of Binomial(n,21​).
(14)
def expected_min_error(n, m):
    """Exact expected smallest training error of m independent coin-flip classifiers, on n training points."""
    k = np.arange(1, n + 1)
    return np.sum((1 - stats.binom.cdf(k - 1, n, 0.5)) ** float(m)) / n


n = 50
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
rows = []
for m in [1, 10, 100, 1_000, 10_000]:
    simulated = rng.binomial(n, 0.5, size=(2000, m)).min(axis=1).mean() / n      # brute force, 2000 repetitions
    rows.append((m, expected_min_error(n, m), simulated))
for m in [100_000, 1_000_000]:
    rows.append((m, expected_min_error(n, m), np.nan))
opt = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["candidates m", "expected best training error (exact)", "simulated"])
opt["true risk of every candidate"] = 0.5
print(opt.round(4).to_string(index=False))
 candidates m  expected best training error (exact)  simulated  true risk of every candidate
            1                                0.5000     0.5010                           0.5
           10                                0.3916     0.3909                           0.5
          100                                0.3244     0.3244                           0.5
         1000                                0.2747     0.2750                           0.5
        10000                                0.2343     0.2351                           0.5
       100000                                0.2000        NaN                           0.5
      1000000                                0.1700        NaN                           0.5

With a single candidate the training error is 0.5, as it should. With a thousand candidates, the best one has a training error of about 0.27; with a million, about 0.17. All of these candidates are useless, with a true risk of exactly 0.5, and the best of them looks like a classifier with 83% accuracy. The simulation (third column) agrees with the exact formula. Figure 3.4 shows the optimism for several sample sizes, and compares it with the simple expression ln⁡m/(2n)\sqrt{\ln m / (2n)}lnm/(2n)​ that we will prove in Section 3.6.

# Figure 3.4 — the optimism of the best of m useless candidates
def figure_3_4():
    ms = np.unique(np.logspace(0, 6, 40).astype(int))
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
    styles = {25: (VERMILION, "-"), 50: (BLUE, "--"), 100: (GREEN, "-."), 400: (PURPLE, ":")}
    for n_, (color, ls) in styles.items():
        gap = [0.5 - expected_min_error(n_, m) for m in ms]
        ax.plot(ms, gap, color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=2, label=f"exact optimism, $n$ = {n_}")
        ax.plot(ms, np.sqrt(np.log(ms) / (2 * n_)), color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=0.9, alpha=0.55)
    ax.plot([], [], color="gray", linewidth=0.9, label=r"$\sqrt{\ln m/(2n)}$ (thin lines)")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="number of candidates $m$", ylabel="true risk minus best training error",
           title="Optimism of the best of $m$ useless candidates")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_4()

Two facts stand out. The optimism grows with the logarithm of the number of candidates (going from a hundred to a million candidates only doubles it), and it shrinks like 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​ when the sample grows. That is the pattern of the theory we are about to develop, and it matches the thin curves of the formula ln⁡m/(2n)\sqrt{\ln m/(2n)}lnm/(2n)​, which will turn out to be an upper bound on this optimism that is nearly attained here.

Pitfall — the winner’s curse

Every time you compare many models, many hyperparameter values or many feature subsets on the same data and keep the best one, you are doing what the experiment above does with mmm coin-flip classifiers: the winner’s score is optimistic, and more so the more you tried. This is exactly the leakage of Section 2.7 (feature selection on the whole data set gave 82% accuracy on pure noise), seen from the theory side. The cure is also the same: keep data that played no role in the selection, a validation set or a test set, to measure the winner (Chapter 5).

3.5 Concentration: from the law of large numbers to Hoeffding’s inequality¶

The law of large numbers says that the empirical risk of a fixed function converges to its true risk, but it does not say how fast, and a guarantee that “eventually” holds is of little use for a data set of 500 examples. We need a statement of the form “with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, the empirical risk is within ε\varepsilonε of the true one, as soon as nnn is at least ...”. Such statements are called concentration inequalities. We build them in three steps, from the crudest to the sharpest.

3.5.1 Markov and Chebyshev¶

Markov’s inequality. If Z≥0Z \ge 0Z≥0 is a random variable and t>0t > 0t>0, then

P(Z≥t)≤E[Z]t.\mathbb{P}(Z \ge t) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[Z]}{t}.P(Z≥t)≤tE[Z]​.
(15)

Proof. Z≥t I[Z≥t]Z \ge t\,\mathbb{I}[Z \ge t]Z≥tI[Z≥t] holds for every outcome, since Z≥0Z \ge 0Z≥0. Take expectations: E[Z]≥t P(Z≥t)\mathbb{E}[Z] \ge t\,\mathbb{P}(Z \ge t)E[Z]≥tP(Z≥t). □\square□

Applied to (Z−E[Z])2(Z - \mathbb{E}[Z])^2(Z−E[Z])2 it gives Chebyshev’s inequality, P(∣Z−E[Z]∣≥t)≤Var⁡(Z)/t2\mathbb{P}(\lvert Z - \mathbb{E}[Z]\rvert \ge t) \le \operatorname{Var}(Z)/t^2P(∣Z−E[Z]∣≥t)≤Var(Z)/t2. For the mean Xˉn\bar X_nXˉn​ of nnn independent variables with mean μ\muμ and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, whose variance is σ2/n\sigma^2/nσ2/n (Section 2.6.2),

P(∣Xˉn−μ∣≥ε)≤σ2nε2.\mathbb{P}\big(\lvert \bar X_n - \mu\rvert \ge \varepsilon\big) \le \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}.P(∣Xˉn​−μ∣≥ε)≤nε2σ2​.
(16)

This is already a non-asymptotic statement, but the probability decays only like 1/n1/n1/n: to be 99% sure we need a hundred times more data than to be 0% sure of nothing. We can do much better if the variables are bounded, as the losses of a classifier are.

3.5.2 The Chernoff method and Hoeffding’s inequality¶

The idea of Chernoff is to apply Markov’s inequality not to ZZZ but to esZe^{sZ}esZ, for a free parameter s>0s > 0s>0 that we choose at the end: since z↦eszz \mapsto e^{sz}z↦esz is increasing,

P(Z≥t)=P(esZ≥est)≤e−st E[esZ].\mathbb{P}(Z \ge t) = \mathbb{P}\big(e^{sZ} \ge e^{st}\big) \le e^{-st}\,\mathbb{E}\big[e^{sZ}\big].P(Z≥t)=P(esZ≥est)≤e−stE[esZ].
(17)

For a sum of independent variables, E[es∑iZi]=∏iE[esZi]\mathbb{E}[e^{s\sum_i Z_i}] = \prod_i \mathbb{E}[e^{sZ_i}]E[es∑i​Zi​]=∏i​E[esZi​] factorizes, and what remains is to bound the moment generating function E[esZi]\mathbb{E}[e^{sZ_i}]E[esZi​] of each term. For a bounded variable this is done by Hoeffding’s lemma.

P(Sn−E[Sn]≥t)≤exp⁡(−2t2∑i(bi−ai)2),\mathbb{P}\big(S_n - \mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge t\big) \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i}(b_i - a_i)^2}\Big),P(Sn​−E[Sn​]≥t)≤exp(−∑i​(bi​−ai​)22t2​),
(22)

and the same bound holds for the lower tail. In particular, for the mean of nnn independent variables with values in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] and expectation μ\muμ,

P(Xˉn−μ≥ε)≤e−2nε2,P(∣Xˉn−μ∣≥ε)≤2 e−2nε2.\mathbb{P}\big(\bar X_n - \mu \ge \varepsilon\big) \le e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}, \qquad \mathbb{P}\big(\lvert \bar X_n - \mu\rvert \ge \varepsilon\big) \le 2\,e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}.P(Xˉn​−μ≥ε)≤e−2nε2,P(∣Xˉn​−μ∣≥ε)≤2e−2nε2.
(23)
Proof of Hoeffding’s inequality (you may skip it)

Apply the Chernoff method to Sn−E[Sn]=∑i(Xi−E[Xi])S_n - \mathbb{E}[S_n] = \sum_i (X_i - \mathbb{E}[X_i])Sn​−E[Sn​]=∑i​(Xi​−E[Xi​]), whose terms are independent, have mean zero, and lie in an interval of length bi−aib_i - a_ibi​−ai​. For any s>0s > 0s>0, by Markov’s inequality, independence, and Hoeffding’s lemma,

P(Sn−E[Sn]≥t)≤e−st∏i=1nE[es(Xi−EXi)]≤exp⁡(−st+s28∑i(bi−ai)2).\mathbb{P}\big(S_n - \mathbb{E}[S_n] \ge t\big) \le e^{-st}\prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\big[e^{s(X_i - \mathbb{E}X_i)}\big] \le \exp\Big(-st + \frac{s^2}{8}\sum_{i}(b_i - a_i)^2\Big).P(Sn​−E[Sn​]≥t)≤e−sti=1∏n​E[es(Xi​−EXi​)]≤exp(−st+8s2​i∑​(bi​−ai​)2).
(24)

The exponent is a quadratic function of sss, minimized at s=4t/∑i(bi−ai)2s = 4t / \sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2s=4t/∑i​(bi​−ai​)2, where it equals −2t2/∑i(bi−ai)2-2t^2/\sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2−2t2/∑i​(bi​−ai​)2. For the mean, take t=nεt = n\varepsilont=nε and ∑i(bi−ai)2=n\sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2 = n∑i​(bi​−ai​)2=n: the bound becomes exp⁡(−2n2ε2/n)=e−2nε2\exp(-2n^2\varepsilon^2/n) = e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}exp(−2n2ε2/n)=e−2nε2. The two-sided bound adds the two tails. □\square□

From the inequality to a guarantee. Fix a function fff before seeing the data, and let the loss be bounded in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] (as the 0–1 loss is). The numbers ℓ(yi,f(xi))\ell(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i))ℓ(yi​,f(xi​)) are i.i.d. with values in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] and mean R(f)R(f)R(f), so

P(∣R^S(f)−R(f)∣≥ε)≤2 e−2nε2.\mathbb{P}\big(\lvert \hat{R}_S(f) - R(f)\rvert \ge \varepsilon\big) \le 2\,e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}.P(∣R^S​(f)−R(f)∣≥ε)≤2e−2nε2.
(25)

Setting the right-hand side equal to δ\deltaδ and solving for ε\varepsilonε gives the equivalent confidence form: with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over the draw of SSS,

 ∣R^S(f)−R(f)∣≤ln⁡(2/δ)2n \boxed{\ \lvert \hat{R}_S(f) - R(f)\rvert \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2n}}\ } ∣R^S​(f)−R(f)∣≤2nln(2/δ)​​ ​
(26)

The deviation shrinks like 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​ and grows only like ln⁡(1/δ)\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}ln(1/δ)​ when we ask for more confidence: being very sure is cheap, being very precise is expensive.

3.5.3 How good are these bounds?¶

Let us compare the bounds with the truth in a case where the truth can be computed exactly: the mean of nnn Bernoulli(0.3) variables, and the probability that it deviates from 0.3 by at least ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1. The exact probability comes from the binomial distribution; we also show the Gaussian approximation of the central limit theorem (Section 2.6.6), which is accurate but is not a guarantee.

p_true, eps = 0.3, 0.1


def exact_tail(n):
    """P(|mean - p| >= eps) for the mean of n Bernoulli(p) variables, from the binomial distribution."""
    lo = np.floor(n * (p_true - eps) + 1e-9)             # k/n <= p - eps   <=>   k <= lo
    hi = np.ceil(n * (p_true + eps) - 1e-9)              # k/n >= p + eps   <=>   k >= hi
    return stats.binom.cdf(lo, n, p_true) + stats.binom.sf(hi - 1, n, p_true)


def tail_table(ns):
    ns = np.asarray(ns)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "n": ns,
        "exact": [exact_tail(n) for n in ns],
        "CLT approximation": 2 * stats.norm.sf(eps * np.sqrt(ns) / np.sqrt(p_true * (1 - p_true))),
        "Hoeffding": np.minimum(1, 2 * np.exp(-2 * ns * eps ** 2)),
        "Chebyshev": np.minimum(1, p_true * (1 - p_true) / (ns * eps ** 2)),
    })


print(tail_table([10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000]).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.5f}"))
   n   exact  CLT approximation  Hoeffding  Chebyshev
  10 0.73317            0.49015    1.00000    1.00000
  20 0.46524            0.32911    1.00000    1.00000
  50 0.16365            0.12282    0.73576    0.42000
 100 0.03745            0.02910    0.27067    0.21000
 200 0.00257            0.00203    0.03663    0.10500
 500 0.00000            0.00000    0.00009    0.04200
1000 0.00000            0.00000    0.00000    0.02100

# Figure 3.5 — the probability of a deviation of 0.1: exact value and bounds
def figure_3_5():
    ns = np.arange(10, 1001, 5)
    tab = tail_table(ns)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
    ax.plot(tab["n"], tab["exact"], color="black", linewidth=2.2, label="exact (binomial)")
    ax.plot(tab["n"], tab["CLT approximation"], color=GREEN, linestyle=":", linewidth=2, label="CLT approximation (not a bound)")
    ax.plot(tab["n"], tab["Hoeffding"], color=BLUE, linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label=r"Hoeffding $2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$")
    ax.plot(tab["n"], tab["Chebyshev"], color=VERMILION, linestyle="-.", linewidth=2, label=r"Chebyshev $\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_ylim(1e-12, 2)
    ax.set(xlabel="sample size $n$", ylabel=r"$\mathbb{P}(|\bar X_n - 0.3| \geq 0.1)$",
           title="A deviation of 0.1 for the mean of Bernoulli(0.3) variables")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_5()

On the logarithmic scale of Figure 3.5 an exponential decay is a straight line. The exact probability (black) decays exponentially, and Hoeffding’s bound (blue dashed) decays at nearly the same exponential rate, staying above the truth by a modest factor: it is a guarantee that is also informative. Chebyshev’s bound (vermilion) decays only polynomially and is useless for large nnn, though it is better than Hoeffding’s for nnn up to about 100 in this table, because Hoeffding uses only the range of the variables, while Chebyshev uses their variance (0.21 here, less than the worst case 0.25 of the range [0,1][0, 1][0,1]). There are sharper inequalities that use both (Bernstein’s, Bennett’s); we do not need them. The Gaussian approximation (green dotted) is the closest to the truth for moderate nnn, but it carries no guarantee: it is an approximation, not an inequality.

Worked example 3.2 — how many coin flips?¶

We want to estimate the probability ppp that a coin lands heads, to within ε=0.05\varepsilon = 0.05ε=0.05, with confidence 1−δ=0.991 - \delta = 0.991−δ=0.99. By Hoeffding, it suffices that 2e−2nε2≤δ2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2} \le \delta2e−2nε2≤δ, that is

n≥ln⁡(2/δ)2ε2=ln⁡2002⋅0.0025=5.2980.005≈1059.7⟹n=1060.n \ge \frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2} = \frac{\ln 200}{2 \cdot 0.0025} = \frac{5.298}{0.005} \approx 1059.7 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n = 1060.n≥2ε2ln(2/δ)​=2⋅0.0025ln200​=0.0055.298​≈1059.7⟹n=1060.
(27)

Chebyshev, in the worst case σ2=14\sigma^2 = \tfrac14σ2=41​, requires n≥1/4ε2δ=10,000n \ge \frac{1/4}{\varepsilon^2\delta} = 10{,}000n≥ε2δ1/4​=10,000. The central limit theorem suggests n≈(z0.995 σ/ε)2=(2.576⋅0.5/0.05)2≈664n \approx (z_{0.995}\,\sigma/\varepsilon)^2 = (2.576 \cdot 0.5/0.05)^2 \approx 664n≈(z0.995​σ/ε)2=(2.576⋅0.5/0.05)2≈664, a number that is right for large nnn but is not guaranteed. Let us compute the three.

eps_c, delta_c = 0.05, 0.01
n_hoeffding = int(np.ceil(np.log(2 / delta_c) / (2 * eps_c ** 2)))
n_chebyshev = int(np.ceil(0.25 / (eps_c ** 2 * delta_c)))
n_clt = int(np.ceil((stats.norm.ppf(1 - delta_c / 2) * 0.5 / eps_c) ** 2))
print(f"Hoeffding (guaranteed)            : n >= {n_hoeffding}")
print(f"Chebyshev (guaranteed, worst case): n >= {n_chebyshev}")
print(f"CLT (approximate)                 : n >= {n_clt}")

# A sanity check of the Hoeffding sample size by simulation (the worst case is p = 1/2)
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
for n_try in (n_clt, n_hoeffding):
    means = rng.binomial(n_try, 0.5, size=200_000) / n_try
    print(f"n = {n_try:>4}: fraction of 200,000 repetitions with |mean - 0.5| > 0.05: {np.mean(np.abs(means - 0.5) > eps_c):.5f}   (target: at most {delta_c})")
Hoeffding (guaranteed)            : n >= 1060
Chebyshev (guaranteed, worst case): n >= 10000
CLT (approximate)                 : n >= 664
n =  664: fraction of 200,000 repetitions with |mean - 0.5| > 0.05: 0.00945   (target: at most 0.01)
n = 1060: fraction of 200,000 repetitions with |mean - 0.5| > 0.05: 0.00111   (target: at most 0.01)

With n=1060n = 1060n=1060 the failure rate is far below the 1% we allowed: Hoeffding’s guarantee is conservative, because it is valid for every distribution on [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. The CLT sample size of 664 gives a failure rate close to the nominal 1%, but that holds only because the Gaussian approximation is excellent for a Bernoulli(½) with n≈664n \approx 664n≈664; for rare events (a probability of 0.01, say) it is much worse.

Key idea

Hoeffding’s inequality is the engine of generalization theory. It turns “the average of nnn bounded independent variables” into “within ln⁡(2/δ)/(2n)\sqrt{\ln(2/\delta)/(2n)}ln(2/δ)/(2n)​ of its mean, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ”. It requires only independence and boundedness: no Gaussianity, no knowledge of the variance. Its two limitations are the topic of the next sections. It speaks about one function fixed in advance (Section 3.6 handles the function chosen by ERM), and it needs a bounded loss (for the squared loss, one needs other tools, which exist but are beyond this book).

3.6 Learning with a finite hypothesis class¶

Section 3.4 showed that Hoeffding’s guarantee for one fixed function cannot be applied to f^S\hat f_Sf^​S​, because f^S\hat f_Sf^​S​ was chosen with the help of the data. The remedy is to ask for more: a bound that holds simultaneously for all functions of H\mathcal{H}H, hence also for the one that the data selected. For a finite class the union bound does it: for any events A1,…,AmA_1, \dots, A_mA1​,…,Am​,

P(⋃j=1mAj)≤∑j=1mP(Aj).\mathbb{P}\Big(\bigcup_{j=1}^m A_j\Big) \le \sum_{j=1}^m \mathbb{P}(A_j).P(j=1⋃m​Aj​)≤j=1∑m​P(Aj​).
(28)

Let H\mathcal{H}H be a finite set with ∣H∣\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert∣H∣ functions and let the loss take values in [0,1][0, 1][0,1].

Theorem 3.1 (uniform deviation for a finite class). For every δ∈(0,1)\delta \in (0, 1)δ∈(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over the draw of the training set SSS of nnn i.i.d. examples, all functions f∈Hf \in \mathcal{H}f∈H satisfy

 ∣R(f)−R^S(f)∣≤ln⁡∣H∣+ln⁡(2/δ)2n \boxed{\ \lvert R(f) - \hat{R}_S(f)\rvert \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert + \ln(2/\delta)}{2n}}\ } ∣R(f)−R^S​(f)∣≤2nln∣H∣+ln(2/δ)​​ ​
(29)

Proof. Let ε\varepsilonε denote the right-hand side. For each fixed fff, Hoeffding’s inequality gives P(∣R(f)−R^S(f)∣>ε)≤2e−2nε2=δ/∣H∣\mathbb{P}(\lvert R(f) - \hat{R}_S(f)\rvert > \varepsilon) \le 2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2} = \delta/\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvertP(∣R(f)−R^S​(f)∣>ε)≤2e−2nε2=δ/∣H∣, because 2nε2=ln⁡∣H∣+ln⁡(2/δ)2n\varepsilon^2 = \ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert + \ln(2/\delta)2nε2=ln∣H∣+ln(2/δ). By the union bound over the ∣H∣\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert∣H∣ functions, the probability that at least one of them deviates by more than ε\varepsilonε is at most ∣H∣⋅δ/∣H∣=δ\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert \cdot \delta / \lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert = \delta∣H∣⋅δ/∣H∣=δ. □\square□

The price of uniformity is the term ln⁡∣H∣\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvertln∣H∣: the size of the class enters only through its logarithm. A class with a million functions costs ln⁡106≈13.8\ln 10^6 \approx 13.8ln106≈13.8; a class with 10100 functions costs 230. This is the mathematical form of the optimism of Section 3.4.1, and it explains why the curves of Figure 3.4 grew like ln⁡m\sqrt{\ln m}lnm​.

Corollary 3.2 (what ERM guarantees). On the event of Theorem 3.1, with ε\varepsilonε its right-hand side, the ERM solution satisfies

R(f^S)≤R(fH)+2ε,that is,estimation error≤2ln⁡∣H∣+ln⁡(2/δ)2n.R(\hat f_S) \le R(f_{\mathcal{H}}) + 2\varepsilon, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad \text{estimation error} \le 2\sqrt{\frac{\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert + \ln(2/\delta)}{2n}}.R(f^​S​)≤R(fH​)+2ε,that is,estimation error≤22nln∣H∣+ln(2/δ)​​.
(30)

Proof. Three inequalities, in a chain: R(f^S)≤R^S(f^S)+εR(\hat f_S) \le \hat{R}_S(\hat f_S) + \varepsilonR(f^​S​)≤R^S​(f^​S​)+ε (uniform deviation, applied to f^S\hat f_Sf^​S​), then R^S(f^S)≤R^S(fH)\hat{R}_S(\hat f_S) \le \hat{R}_S(f_{\mathcal{H}})R^S​(f^​S​)≤R^S​(fH​) (definition of ERM), then R^S(fH)≤R(fH)+ε\hat{R}_S(f_{\mathcal{H}}) \le R(f_{\mathcal{H}}) + \varepsilonR^S​(fH​)≤R(fH​)+ε (uniform deviation, applied to fHf_{\mathcal{H}}fH​). □\square□

So the estimation error of ERM over a finite class shrinks like ln⁡∣H∣/n\sqrt{\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert / n}ln∣H∣/n​: the more candidates, the more data are needed, but only logarithmically in the number of candidates. Inverting the formulas gives the sample complexity: to have all deviations at most ε\varepsilonε, or an estimation error at most ε\varepsilonε (which needs deviations of ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2), it suffices that

n≥ln⁡∣H∣+ln⁡(2/δ)2ε2orn≥2 (ln⁡∣H∣+ln⁡(2/δ))ε2respectively.n \ge \frac{\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert + \ln(2/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2} \qquad\text{or}\qquad n \ge \frac{2\,\big(\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert + \ln(2/\delta)\big)}{\varepsilon^2} \quad\text{respectively.}n≥2ε2ln∣H∣+ln(2/δ)​orn≥ε22(ln∣H∣+ln(2/δ))​respectively.
(31)

Worked example 3.3 — a class described by 20 bits¶

Suppose the hypotheses are the classifiers that can be described by 20 binary choices (for instance, 20 yes/no design decisions), so that ∣H∣=220≈106\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert = 2^{20} \approx 10^6∣H∣=220≈106. How many examples guarantee, with probability 0.99, that every empirical risk is within ε=0.05\varepsilon = 0.05ε=0.05 of the true one?

n≥20ln⁡2+ln⁡2002⋅0.052=13.863+5.2980.005≈3832.2⟹n=3833.n \ge \frac{20\ln 2 + \ln 200}{2 \cdot 0.05^2} = \frac{13.863 + 5.298}{0.005} \approx 3832.2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n = 3833.n≥2⋅0.05220ln2+ln200​=0.00513.863+5.298​≈3832.2⟹n=3833.
(32)

To guarantee an estimation error of 0.05 for ERM we need four times as many: n≥2⋅19.161/0.0025≈15,329n \ge 2 \cdot 19.161/0.0025 \approx 15{,}329n≥2⋅19.161/0.0025≈15,329, that is n=15,330n = 15{,}330n=15,330. Notice the shape of the result: a model that is described by bbb bits has ln⁡∣H∣=bln⁡2\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert = b \ln 2ln∣H∣=bln2, so the required number of examples grows linearly with the number of bits, and a model with ppp real parameters stored with 32 bits has at most 232p2^{32p}232p different functions, so nnn grows linearly with the number of parameters ppp. This is the first appearance of a rule that we will meet again in a sharper form: the number of examples must be larger than the capacity of the model.

def n_uniform(log_h, eps, delta, estimation=False):
    """Sample size from Theorem 3.1 (uniform deviation <= eps) or from Corollary 3.2 (estimation error <= eps)."""
    base = (log_h + np.log(2 / delta)) / (2 * eps ** 2)
    return int(np.ceil(4 * base if estimation else base))


print("|H| = 2^20, eps = 0.05, delta = 0.01")
print("  uniform deviation <= 0.05    :", n_uniform(20 * np.log(2), 0.05, 0.01))
print("  ERM estimation error <= 0.05 :", n_uniform(20 * np.log(2), 0.05, 0.01, estimation=True))
for p_params in (10, 100, 1000):
    print(f"a model with {p_params:>4} parameters of 32 bits: n >= {n_uniform(32 * p_params * np.log(2), 0.05, 0.01):,}")

3.6.1 An experiment on real data: decision stumps¶

A decision stump is the simplest classifier on a table: it looks at one feature, compares it with a threshold, and predicts one class on each side. On the Breast Cancer data we build a finite class H\mathcal{H}H by taking each of the 30 features, 19 thresholds (the 5th, 10th, ..., 95th percentiles of the feature) and 2 possible orientations: ∣H∣=30⋅19⋅2=1140\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert = 30 \cdot 19 \cdot 2 = 1140∣H∣=30⋅19⋅2=1140 stumps.

To check Theorem 3.1 we need to know the true risk of every stump, which requires knowing D\mathcal{D}D. We therefore declare that D\mathcal{D}D is the empirical distribution of the 569 patients, which puts probability 1/5691/5691/569 on each patient. The true risk of a stump is then its error rate on the 569 patients, computed exactly, and a “training set” of size nnn is nnn patients drawn with replacement (so the draws are i.i.d. from D\mathcal{D}D, as the theory requires; nnn may even exceed 569). This is a standard device, called the bootstrap world: a real data set, with a population that we know completely.

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer

bc = load_breast_cancer()
X_bc, y_bc = bc.data, bc.target
N_BC, D_BC = X_bc.shape

# The finite class of stumps: one column of ERR per stump, holding 1 where the stump errs on a patient
columns, stump_info = [], []
for j in range(D_BC):
    for thr in np.quantile(X_bc[:, j], np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19)):
        for orientation in (0, 1):
            pred = (X_bc[:, j] > thr) if orientation == 0 else (X_bc[:, j] <= thr)
            columns.append(pred.astype(int) != y_bc)
            stump_info.append((j, thr, orientation))
ERR = np.array(columns).T.astype(float)              # shape (569, 1140)
R_TRUE = ERR.mean(axis=0)                            # the exact true risk of every stump under D
H_SIZE = ERR.shape[1]
best = R_TRUE.argmin()
print(f"|H| = {H_SIZE} stumps | best stump: feature '{bc.feature_names[stump_info[best][0]]}', true risk {R_TRUE[best]:.4f}")
|H| = 1140 stumps | best stump: feature 'worst perimeter', true risk 0.0826

def uniform_bound(n, h_size, delta=0.05):
    return np.sqrt((np.log(h_size) + np.log(2 / delta)) / (2 * n))


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
delta_s = 0.05
rows = []
for n in [20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000]:
    counts = rng.multinomial(n, np.ones(N_BC) / N_BC, size=3000)     # 3000 training sets of n patients, with replacement
    R_hat = counts @ ERR / n                                         # empirical risk of every stump on every training set
    sup_dev = np.abs(R_hat - R_TRUE).max(axis=1)                     # largest deviation over the whole class
    erm = R_hat.argmin(axis=1)                                       # ERM stump of each training set
    bound = uniform_bound(n, H_SIZE, delta_s)
    rows.append({"n": n, "95th percentile of sup deviation": np.quantile(sup_dev, 1 - delta_s), "Theorem 3.1 bound": bound,
                 "runs above the bound": np.mean(sup_dev > bound), "training error of ERM": R_hat.min(axis=1).mean(),
                 "true risk of ERM": R_TRUE[erm].mean(), "best stump": R_TRUE.min()})
stump_results = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(stump_results.round(4).to_string(index=False))
   n  95th percentile of sup deviation  Theorem 3.1 bound  runs above the bound  training error of ERM  true risk of ERM  best stump

  50                            0.2403             0.3275                0.0010                 0.0423            0.1039      0.0826
 100                            0.1733             0.2316                0.0007                 0.0554            0.0941      0.0826
 200                            0.1220             0.1638                0.0003                 0.0651            0.0897      0.0826
 500                            0.0764             0.1036                0.0003                 0.0735            0.0874      0.0826
1000                            0.0537             0.0732                0.0003                 0.0773            0.0863      0.0826
2000                            0.0385             0.0518                0.0003                 0.0797            0.0854      0.0826

# Figure 3.6 — finite-class theory on the stumps of the Breast Cancer data
def figure_3_6():
    r = stump_results
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.3))

    ax = axes[0]
    ax.plot(r["n"], r["Theorem 3.1 bound"], color=BLUE, marker="s", linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="bound of Theorem 3.1 ($\\delta$ = 0.05)")
    ax.plot(r["n"], r["95th percentile of sup deviation"], color=VERMILION, marker="o", linewidth=2, label="observed: 95th percentile of the largest deviation")
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="training-set size $n$", ylabel="largest deviation over the class", title="(a) the bound holds, and is not far off")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)

    ax = axes[1]
    ax.plot(r["n"], r["training error of ERM"], color=ORANGE, marker="^", linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="training error of ERM")
    ax.plot(r["n"], r["true risk of ERM"], color=GREEN, marker="o", linewidth=2, label="true risk of ERM")
    ax.axhline(R_TRUE.min(), color="black", linewidth=1.2)
    ax.text(21, R_TRUE.min() + 0.002, "best stump (best in class)", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="training-set size $n$", ylabel="0-1 risk", title="(b) ERM: optimism and convergence")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_6()

Four observations.

  1. The bound is valid. The largest deviation exceeds the bound of Theorem 3.1 in a tiny fraction of the runs (column “runs above the bound”), far below the 5% that we allowed. This is not a coincidence: the guarantee uses Hoeffding’s inequality and the union bound, both of which are conservative.

  2. The bound is not far from the truth, within a factor 1.3 to 1.4 at every sample size, and it has the right shape, 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​. Stumps on correlated features behave as if the class had fewer than 1140 independent members, which is one reason the bound is not attained.

  3. The training error is optimistic, the test error is pessimistic, and they close in on the best stump from opposite sides (panel b): this is the chain of inequalities of Section 3.4 made visible. With n=100n = 100n=100 the ERM stump has a training error of 5.5% but a true risk of 9.4%.

  4. The ERM guarantee of Corollary 3.2 is very loose here. On average, the excess risk of the ERM stump over the best stump is below 0.005 for n=500n = 500n=500, while the guarantee 2ε2\varepsilon2ε is 0.21 at that sample size. The guarantee is about the worst case, and our real data are not that bad.

Try it

Make the class smaller (use 5 thresholds per feature instead of 19) or larger (use 99 thresholds). By how much does the bound of Theorem 3.1 change? Does the observed deviation change by a comparable amount? Since the bound depends on the class only through ln⁡∣H∣\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvertln∣H∣, multiplying the number of stumps by five should increase it by a small factor.

3.7 Infinite classes: the VC dimension¶

Theorem 3.1 is of no use for the most important classes of the book: there are infinitely many lines in the plane, so ln⁡∣H∣=∞\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert = \inftyln∣H∣=∞. Yet the lines are clearly less flexible than “all functions”, and the experiments of Section 3.3 showed that a class with 5 features behaves very differently from one with 44. We need a measure of the effective size of a class. The key observation is that a sample of nnn points can only distinguish between the different label vectors that the class produces on those nnn points. There are at most 2n2^n2n of them, no matter how large H\mathcal{H}H is. If a class produces fewer than 2n2^n2n, the class is not completely flexible on nnn points, and the count of label vectors can play the role of ∣H∣\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert∣H∣.

3.7.1 Dichotomies, growth function, shattering¶

Throughout this section the labels are binary and the loss is the 0–1 loss. For nnn points x1,…,xn\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_nx1​,…,xn​, the set of dichotomies (labelings) that H\mathcal{H}H can produce on them is

H(x1,…,xn)={(f(x1),…,f(xn)):f∈H}⊆{0,1}n.\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_n) = \big\{(f(\mathbf{x}_1), \dots, f(\mathbf{x}_n)) : f \in \mathcal{H}\big\} \subseteq \{0, 1\}^n .H(x1​,…,xn​)={(f(x1​),…,f(xn​)):f∈H}⊆{0,1}n.
(33)

The growth function is the largest number of dichotomies on any nnn points,

ΠH(n)=max⁡x1,…,xn ∣H(x1,…,xn)∣ ≤ 2n.\Pi_{\mathcal{H}}(n) = \max_{\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_n}\ \big\lvert \mathcal{H}(\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_n)\big\rvert \ \le\ 2^n .ΠH​(n)=x1​,…,xn​max​ ∣∣​H(x1​,…,xn​)∣∣​ ≤ 2n.
(34)

A set of nnn points is shattered by H\mathcal{H}H if H\mathcal{H}H produces all 2n2^n2n labelings on it. The VC dimension (Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension) of H\mathcal{H}H, written dVCd_{\mathrm{VC}}dVC​, is the size of the largest set that H\mathcal{H}H can shatter, that is, the largest nnn with ΠH(n)=2n\Pi_{\mathcal{H}}(n) = 2^nΠH​(n)=2n; it is ∞\infty∞ if arbitrarily large sets can be shattered.

Two words of caution. To show that dVC≥dd_{\mathrm{VC}} \ge ddVC​≥d it is enough to find one set of ddd points that can be shattered. To show that dVC<d+1d_{\mathrm{VC}} < d + 1dVC​<d+1 we must show that no set of d+1d + 1d+1 points can be shattered. The two tasks are not symmetric.

Worked example 3.4 — intervals on a line¶

Let H\mathcal{H}H be the intervals of the real line, fa,b(x)=I[a≤x≤b]f_{a, b}(x) = \mathbb{I}[a \le x \le b]fa,b​(x)=I[a≤x≤b]: a point gets label 1 inside the interval and 0 outside. Take nnn distinct points and sort them, x1<⋯<xnx_1 < \dots < x_nx1​<⋯<xn​. A labeling is produced by some interval if and only if its ones are consecutive (a single block of ones, or no ones at all). A block is determined by where it starts and where it ends, which is a choice of two of the n+1n + 1n+1 “gaps” between consecutive points (counting the two ends), so there are (n+12)=n(n+1)2\binom{n+1}{2} = \tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}(2n+1​)=2n(n+1)​ non-empty blocks, plus the empty labeling:

ΠH(n)=n(n+1)2+1.\Pi_{\mathcal{H}}(n) = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} + 1 .ΠH​(n)=2n(n+1)​+1.
(35)

For n=2n = 2n=2 this is 4=224 = 2^24=22: two points are shattered. For n=3n = 3n=3 it is 7<87 < 87<8: the labeling (1,0,1)(1, 0, 1)(1,0,1) cannot be produced, since a single interval that contains x1x_1x1​ and x3x_3x3​ also contains x2x_2x2​. Hence dVC=2d_{\mathrm{VC}} = 2dVC​=2 for the intervals. The same reasoning shows dVC=1d_{\mathrm{VC}} = 1dVC​=1 for the half-lines I[x>t]\mathbb{I}[x > t]I[x>t], whose growth function is n+1n + 1n+1. Let us verify the count by brute force.

def count_dichotomies_intervals(n):
    """Distinct label vectors produced on the points 0, 1, ..., n-1 by the intervals [a, b] (and the empty interval)."""
    xs = np.arange(n)
    ends = np.arange(-0.5, n, 1.0)                      # an interval end can sit in any of the n + 1 gaps
    labelings = {tuple((xs >= a) & (xs <= b)) for a in ends for b in ends}   # a > b gives the empty interval
    return len(labelings)


pd.DataFrame({"n": range(1, 9),
              "2^n": [2 ** k for k in range(1, 9)],
              "intervals, counted": [count_dichotomies_intervals(k) for k in range(1, 9)],
              "n(n+1)/2 + 1": [k * (k + 1) // 2 + 1 for k in range(1, 9)]}).set_index("n")
Loading...

The counted values coincide with the formula; they equal 2n2^n2n for n=1,2n = 1, 2n=1,2 and fall below it from n=3n = 3n=3 on. After the first failure the growth function becomes a polynomial in nnn (here quadratic), while 2n2^n2n is exponential: this is the general pattern that Theorem 3.3 will state.

3.7.2 Linear classifiers in the plane and in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd¶

Consider the classifiers f(x)=I[w⊤x+b>0]f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{I}[\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b > 0]f(x)=I[w⊤x+b>0] on Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd (linear classifiers, or half-spaces). In the plane (d=2d = 2d=2) any three points that are not on a line can be shattered: whichever subset of them we want to label 1, a line separates it from the rest. Four points cannot be shattered. If they form the corners of a square and we label opposite corners alike (the XOR pattern of Section 1.3), no line separates the two classes; and for four points in any other position some other labeling fails. So dVC=3=d+1d_{\mathrm{VC}} = 3 = d + 1dVC​=3=d+1 in the plane.

The general statement is a classical theorem of Cover (1965), which counts exactly how many of the 2n2^n2n labelings of nnn points in general position (no d+1d + 1d+1 of them on a common hyperplane, the typical situation) are produced by half-spaces of Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd:

Π(n)=2∑k=0d(n−1k).(Cover)\Pi(n) = 2\sum_{k=0}^{d}\binom{n - 1}{k}. \qquad\text{(Cover)}Π(n)=2k=0∑d​(kn−1​).(Cover)
(36)

For n≤d+1n \le d + 1n≤d+1 the sum contains all the binomial coefficients and equals 2⋅2n−1=2n2 \cdot 2^{n-1} = 2^n2⋅2n−1=2n: all labelings are possible. For n=d+2n = d + 2n=d+2 it is 2n−22^n - 22n−2: exactly two labelings are lost. Hence dVC=d+1d_{\mathrm{VC}} = d + 1dVC​=d+1: a linear classifier in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd has d+1d + 1d+1 degrees of freedom (the weights and the bias), and that is also its VC dimension.

We can check Cover’s formula numerically, because deciding whether a labeling is realized by a line is a linear program: we look for (w,b)(\mathbf{w}, b)(w,b) with yi(w⊤xi+b)≥1y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) \ge 1yi​(w⊤xi​+b)≥1 for all iii (with labels yi∈{−1,+1}y_i \in \{-1, +1\}yi​∈{−1,+1}; the margin 1 is only a normalization, since any separating w,b\mathbf{w}, bw,b can be rescaled). The function is_separable below solves it with scipy.optimize.linprog, and we count the separable labelings of random points.

from itertools import product
from math import comb

from scipy.optimize import linprog


def is_separable(X, y):
    """Is there (w, b) with y_i (w.x_i + b) >= 1 for every i?  y in {-1, +1}. A feasibility linear program."""
    n, d = X.shape
    A_ub = -(y[:, None] * np.hstack([X, np.ones((n, 1))]))          # -y_i (x_i, 1) . (w, b) <= -1
    res = linprog(np.zeros(d + 1), A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=-np.ones(n), bounds=[(None, None)] * (d + 1), method="highs")
    return res.status == 0


def cover_count(n, d):
    return 2 * sum(comb(n - 1, k) for k in range(d + 1))


rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
rows = []
for d in (2, 3):
    for n in range(2, 10):
        X = rng.normal(size=(n, d))                                  # random points are in general position
        counted = sum(is_separable(X, np.array(labels)) for labels in product([-1, 1], repeat=n))
        rows.append({"d": d, "n": n, "2^n": 2 ** n, "separable labelings (counted)": counted, "Cover's formula": cover_count(n, d)})
growth_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(growth_table.to_string(index=False))

The counted numbers agree with Cover’s formula in every row. In the plane (d=2d = 2d=2), the number of separable labelings is 8=238 = 2^38=23 for three points, but only 14 of 16 for four points, 22 of 32 for five, 58 of 256 for eight: after n=3n = 3n=3 the fraction of realizable labelings collapses. In space (d=3d = 3d=3) the first loss appears at n=5n = 5n=5 (30 of 32). The class is as rich as its dimension says, and no richer.

3.7.3 A linear classifier can fit pure noise¶

A direct consequence of Cover’s formula is a result that explains Section 3.4 for linear models. Take nnn points in general position and give them random labels: no relation between inputs and labels, nothing to learn. The probability that a linear classifier in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd can still reproduce the labels exactly, hence achieve a training error of zero, is the fraction of realizable labelings:

P(separable)=Π(n)2n=22n∑k=0d(n−1k)=P(Bin(n−1,12)≤d).\mathbb{P}(\text{separable}) = \frac{\Pi(n)}{2^n} = \frac{2}{2^{n}}\sum_{k=0}^{d}\binom{n-1}{k} = \mathbb{P}\big(\mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, \tfrac12) \le d\big).P(separable)=2nΠ(n)​=2n2​k=0∑d​(kn−1​)=P(Bin(n−1,21​)≤d).
(37)

The last equality says that the transition is governed by a binomial distribution centered at (n−1)/2(n-1)/2(n−1)/2: the probability is small when d<n/2−1d < n/2 - 1d<n/2−1, one half at d≈n/2d \approx n/2d≈n/2, and close to one once ddd is a few standard deviations (n/2\sqrt{n}/2n​/2) larger. A linear classifier can memorize random labels as soon as it has about half as many features as there are examples. We test the prediction with n=40n = 40n=40 points and random labels, for dimensions ddd from 5 to 39, with 150 random trials each.

n_noise = 40
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
dims = [5, 10, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 25, 30, 39]
rows = []
for d in dims:
    hits = 0
    for _ in range(150):
        X = rng.normal(size=(n_noise, d))
        y = rng.choice([-1, 1], size=n_noise)                        # pure noise: the labels ignore the features
        hits += is_separable(X, y)
    rows.append({"dimension d": d, "fraction of noise sets fitted perfectly": hits / 150,
                 "theory: P(Bin(39, 1/2) <= d)": stats.binom.cdf(d, n_noise - 1, 0.5)})
noise_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(noise_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))

def figure_3_7():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.4))

figure_3_7()

Panel (a): the number of labelings of the lines follows 2n2^n2n up to n=3n = 3n=3 (the points of the table and the dashed line coincide with the black curve) and then bends away, growing only like n2n^2n2. Panel (b): the simulation (circles) lies on Cover’s curve. For d=5d = 5d=5 or 10 a linear classifier never fits 40 random labels; at d=19d = 19d=19, about half the time; for d=30d = 30d=30 always. This is the mathematical mechanism of overfitting in linear models: with ddd comparable to nnn the classifier has enough freedom to fit anything, noise included, and a perfect training score proves nothing (compare with the optimism of Section 3.4 and with the experiment of Section 2.7, where we selected 10 features out of 2000 on pure noise).

3.7.4 The Sauer–Shelah lemma and the VC bound¶

In the intervals and the lines, the growth function equals 2n2^n2n for a while and then becomes polynomial. This is a theorem: it holds for every class.

Theorem 3.3 (Sauer–Shelah lemma). If H\mathcal{H}H has VC dimension d<∞d < \inftyd<∞, then for every n≥dn \ge dn≥d

ΠH(n)≤∑k=0d(nk)≤(e nd)d.\Pi_{\mathcal{H}}(n) \le \sum_{k=0}^{d}\binom{n}{k} \le \Big(\frac{e\,n}{d}\Big)^{d}.ΠH​(n)≤k=0∑d​(kn​)≤(den​)d.
(38)

(We omit the proof, a short induction; see the book of Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David.) There is no intermediate regime: a class either shatters sets of every size (dVC=∞d_{\mathrm{VC}} = \inftydVC​=∞, and then no uniform guarantee is possible) or its growth function is bounded by a polynomial of degree dVCd_{\mathrm{VC}}dVC​. A polynomial in nnn has a logarithm that grows like dln⁡nd \ln ndlnn, which is exactly what is needed to replace ln⁡∣H∣\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvertln∣H∣ in Theorem 3.1.

Theorem 3.4 (VC generalization bound; Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971). Let H\mathcal{H}H have VC dimension d<∞d < \inftyd<∞, and let the loss be the 0–1 loss. For every δ∈(0,1)\delta \in (0, 1)δ∈(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over the draw of SSS, all f∈Hf \in \mathcal{H}f∈H satisfy, for n≥dn \ge dn≥d,

R(f)≤R^S(f)+8n(d ln⁡2end+ln⁡4δ).R(f) \le \hat{R}_S(f) + \sqrt{\frac{8}{n}\Big(d\,\ln\frac{2en}{d} + \ln\frac{4}{\delta}\Big)}.R(f)≤R^S​(f)+n8​(dlnd2en​+lnδ4​)​.
(39)

The proof replaces the union bound over ∣H∣\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert∣H∣ functions by one over the ΠH(2n)\Pi_{\mathcal{H}}(2n)ΠH​(2n) dichotomies on a double sample of 2n2n2n points (a “symmetrization” argument) and then applies Theorem 3.3; it is beyond the scope of this book (see the Further reading). The constants (8, 4, 2) differ in different textbooks and do not matter; the structure does:

  • the complexity term grows like dln⁡n/n\sqrt{d\ln n / n}dlnn/n​: the number of examples must be larger than the VC dimension, which for linear classifiers is the number of features plus one;

  • the class enters only through dVCd_{\mathrm{VC}}dVC​, so the bound holds for every distribution D\mathcal{D}D and any algorithm that picks a function of H\mathcal{H}H;

  • a rule of thumb that comes out of it, and is often quoted, is that one needs on the order of ten examples per unit of VC dimension for the guarantee to be meaningful. We now see how meaningful it is.

def vc_term(n, d_vc, delta=0.05):
    """The complexity term of Theorem 3.4 (valid for n >= d_vc)."""
    n = np.asarray(n, dtype=float)
    return np.sqrt(8 / n * (d_vc * np.log(2 * np.e * n / d_vc) + np.log(4 / delta)))


def first_n_below(d_vc, level):
    grid = np.logspace(np.log10(d_vc), 10, 40_000)
    return grid[np.argmax(vc_term(grid, d_vc) <= level)]


rows = []
for d_vc in (3, 11, 31, 101):
    rows.append({"VC dimension": d_vc, "term at n = 455": float(vc_term(455, d_vc)),
                 "n needed for term <= 0.5": first_n_below(d_vc, 0.5), "n needed for term <= 0.1": first_n_below(d_vc, 0.1)})
vc_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(vc_table.round(2).to_string(index=False, formatters={"n needed for term <= 0.5": "{:,.0f}".format, "n needed for term <= 0.1": "{:,.0f}".format}))
