# Figure 3.8 — the complexity term of the VC bound
def figure_3_8():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))
    styles = {3: (VERMILION, "-"), 11: (ORANGE, "--"), 31: (BLUE, "-."), 101: (GREEN, ":")}
    for d_vc, (color, ls) in styles.items():
        ns = np.logspace(np.log10(d_vc), 8, 400)
        ax.plot(ns, vc_term(ns, d_vc), color=color, linestyle=ls, linewidth=2, label=f"$d_{{VC}}$ = {d_vc}")
    ax.axhline(1.0, color="black", linewidth=1.2)
    ax.text(1.5e8, 1.12, "above 1 the bound says nothing (an error is at most 1)", fontsize=9, ha="right")
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_ylim(1e-2, 20)
    ax.set(xlabel="training-set size $n$", ylabel="complexity term of the VC bound ($\\delta$ = 0.05)",
           title="The VC bound is informative only for large $n$")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_8()

The message of the table and of Figure 3.8 is sobering and important. Even for a line in the plane (dVC=3d_{\mathrm{VC}} = 3dVC​=3) the guarantee is below 0.5 only after about 800 examples; for a linear classifier on the 30 features of the Breast Cancer data (dVC=31d_{\mathrm{VC}} = 31dVC​=31) it takes more than 7000 examples to get below 0.5, and more than 270,000 to get below 0.1. With the 455 training examples of a typical split, the term is 1.57: the “guarantee” is vacuous (it exceeds 1, and any error is at most 1). The VC bound is worst-case over all distributions and all algorithms, with generous constants, and for any real data set it is far from the truth, as Section 3.10 will measure. Its value is qualitative: it tells us what the generalization gap depends on (ddd and nnn, through dln⁡n/n\sqrt{d\ln n/n}dlnn/n​) and proves that the class of linear classifiers can generalize, whatever the dimension, when nnn is large enough.

Pitfall — parameters are not capacity

For linear classifiers the VC dimension equals the number of parameters, and this has led to the folk rule “capacity = number of parameters”. It is false in general. The one-parameter family fω(x)=I[sin⁡(ωx)>0]f_\omega(x) = \mathbb{I}[\sin(\omega x) > 0]fω​(x)=I[sin(ωx)>0] has an infinite VC dimension: for any nnn one can choose nnn points that it shatters (Exercise 3.8). Conversely, a model with millions of parameters can have a small effective capacity if its parameters are constrained, which is exactly the subject of the next section, and which is why neural networks with more parameters than training examples can still generalize (Chapter 15).

3.8 Rademacher complexity and the role of the norm¶

The VC dimension of a linear classifier grows with the dimension ddd, so the bound of Theorem 3.4 is empty when d≥nd \ge nd≥n. Yet ridge regression, support vector machines and kernel methods work well with d≫nd \gg nd≫n (text with hundreds of thousands of word features, images, or the infinite-dimensional features of Chapter 9). What controls their capacity is not the dimension but the size of the weights, as we will see. To state this precisely we need a measure of capacity that depends on the norm of the weights and on the data, not only on the number of parameters. It is the Rademacher complexity.

3.8.1 Definition: how well can the class fit random signs?¶

A Rademacher variable is a random sign, equal to +1 or -1 with probability 12\tfrac1221​ each. Let σ1,…,σn\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_nσ1​,…,σn​ be independent Rademacher variables. For a class F\mathcal{F}F of real-valued functions and a sample x1,…,xn\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_nx1​,…,xn​, the empirical Rademacher complexity is

R^S(F)=Eσ[ sup⁡f∈F 1n∑i=1nσif(xi)],\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\mathcal{F}) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\sigma}\Big[\ \sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}}\ \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)\Big],R^S​(F)=Eσ​[ f∈Fsup​ n1​i=1∑n​σi​f(xi​)],
(40)

and the Rademacher complexity Rn(F)\mathfrak{R}_n(\mathcal{F})Rn​(F) is its expectation over the random sample. Read the definition as an experiment: assign random labels σi∈{±1}\sigma_i \in \{\pm 1\}σi​∈{±1} to the points, find the function of the class that correlates best with them, and average the best correlation over the random labels. A class that can correlate well with pure noise is rich (it can fit noise, as the lines did in Section 3.7.3); a class that cannot is poor. It is the same idea as the VC dimension, but it measures how well the class fits noise on this sample, not only whether it can fit it perfectly.

Theorem 3.5 (generalization bound with Rademacher complexity). Let G\mathcal{G}G be a class of functions with values in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] (think of g(x,y)=ℓ(y,f(x))g(\mathbf{x}, y) = \ell(y, f(\mathbf{x}))g(x,y)=ℓ(y,f(x)) for f∈Hf \in \mathcal{H}f∈H and a bounded loss). For every δ∈(0,1)\delta \in (0, 1)δ∈(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over the draw of nnn i.i.d. examples, all g∈Gg \in \mathcal{G}g∈G satisfy

E[g]≤1n∑i=1ng(zi)+2 Rn(G)+ln⁡(1/δ)2n,\mathbb{E}[g] \le \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(\mathbf{z}_i) + 2\,\mathfrak{R}_n(\mathcal{G}) + \sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}} ,E[g]≤n1​i=1∑n​g(zi​)+2Rn​(G)+2nln(1/δ)​​,
(41)

and the same holds with Rn(G)\mathfrak{R}_n(\mathcal{G})Rn​(G) replaced by the computable R^S(G)\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\mathcal{G})R^S​(G), provided the last term is replaced by 3ln⁡(2/δ)/(2n)3\sqrt{\ln(2/\delta)/(2n)}3ln(2/δ)/(2n)​. The proof combines a symmetrization step with McDiarmid’s bounded-difference inequality, a relative of Hoeffding’s (Bartlett and Mendelson, 2002; Mohri et al., 2018, Theorem 3.3). Compared with Theorem 3.1, the term ln⁡∣H∣/(2n)\sqrt{\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert/(2n)}ln∣H∣/(2n)​ has been replaced by twice the Rademacher complexity.

Two tools make the theorem usable. The first is the contraction lemma (Ledoux and Talagrand): if φ:R→R\varphi: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}φ:R→R is LLL-Lipschitz, then R^S(φ∘F)≤L R^S(F)\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\varphi \circ \mathcal{F}) \le L\,\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\mathcal{F})R^S​(φ∘F)≤LR^S​(F), so composing the functions with a Lipschitz loss does not increase the complexity by more than the Lipschitz constant. The second is a direct computation for the class that matters most.

3.8.2 Linear functions with a bounded norm¶

Proposition 3.6. Let FB={x↦w⊤x:∥w∥2≤B}\mathcal{F}_B = \{\mathbf{x} \mapsto \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} : \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le B\}FB​={x↦w⊤x:∥w∥2​≤B} and let the sample satisfy ∥xi∥2≤R\lVert\mathbf{x}_i\rVert_2 \le R∥xi​∥2​≤R for all iii. Then

R^S(FB)=Bn Eσ∥∑i=1nσixi∥2 ≤ Bn∑i=1n∥xi∥22 ≤ B Rn.\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\mathcal{F}_B) = \frac{B}{n}\,\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\sigma}\Big\lVert\sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i\mathbf{x}_i\Big\rVert_2 \ \le\ \frac{B}{n}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n\lVert\mathbf{x}_i\rVert_2^2} \ \le\ \frac{B\,R}{\sqrt{n}} .R^S​(FB​)=nB​Eσ​∥∥​i=1∑n​σi​xi​∥∥​2​ ≤ nB​i=1∑n​∥xi​∥22​​ ≤ n​BR​.
(42)

Proof. For a fixed sign vector, sup⁡∥w∥≤B w⊤(1n∑iσixi)\sup_{\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\le B}\ \mathbf{w}^\top\big(\tfrac1n\sum_i\sigma_i\mathbf{x}_i\big)sup∥w∥≤B​ w⊤(n1​∑i​σi​xi​) is the largest value of a dot product over a ball. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality it is at most B ∥1n∑iσixi∥2B\,\lVert\tfrac1n\sum_i\sigma_i\mathbf{x}_i\rVert_2B∥n1​∑i​σi​xi​∥2​, and it is equal to it for w=Bu/∥u∥\mathbf{w} = B\mathbf{u}/\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVertw=Bu/∥u∥ with u=∑iσixi\mathbf{u} = \sum_i\sigma_i\mathbf{x}_iu=∑i​σi​xi​. This gives the first equality. Next, Jensen’s inequality for the concave function ⋅\sqrt{\cdot}⋅​ gives E∥u∥≤E∥u∥2\mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert \le \sqrt{\mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^2}E∥u∥≤E∥u∥2​, and

E∥u∥2=∑i,jE[σiσj] xi⊤xj=∑i∥xi∥2,\mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^2 = \sum_{i, j}\mathbb{E}[\sigma_i\sigma_j]\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j = \sum_{i}\lVert\mathbf{x}_i\rVert^2,E∥u∥2=i,j∑​E[σi​σj​]xi⊤​xj​=i∑​∥xi​∥2,
(43)

because E[σiσj]=0\mathbb{E}[\sigma_i\sigma_j] = 0E[σi​σj​]=0 for i≠ji \ne ji=j and 1 for i=ji = ji=j. Finally ∑i∥xi∥2≤nR2\sum_i\lVert\mathbf{x}_i\rVert^2 \le nR^2∑i​∥xi​∥2≤nR2. □\square□

The result is remarkable. The complexity of the linear class does not depend on the dimension ddd: it depends on the radius BBB of the weights, the radius RRR of the data, and nnn, and it shrinks like 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​. A linear model in a million dimensions with ∥w∥≤B\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert \le B∥w∥≤B is exactly as hard to estimate as one in two dimensions, if the data have the same radius. (If we bound the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ norm instead, ∥w∥1≤B\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1 \le B∥w∥1​≤B, the complexity depends on the dimension only through ln⁡d\sqrt{\ln d}lnd​; this is why sparse methods can handle many more features than examples, Chapter 10 and Exercise 3.9.)

Worked example 3.5 — a Rademacher complexity by hand¶

Take two real points x1=1x_1 = 1x1​=1, x2=2x_2 = 2x2​=2 and the class FB={x↦wx:∣w∣≤B}\mathcal{F}_B = \{x \mapsto wx : \lvert w\rvert \le B\}FB​={x↦wx:∣w∣≤B}. By the first equality of Proposition 3.6,

R^S(FB)=B2 E∣σ1+2σ2∣.\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\mathcal{F}_B) = \frac{B}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\big\lvert\sigma_1 + 2\sigma_2\big\rvert .R^S​(FB​)=2B​E∣∣​σ1​+2σ2​∣∣​.
(44)

The four equally likely sign vectors give ∣σ1+2σ2∣=3,1,1,3\lvert\sigma_1 + 2\sigma_2\rvert = 3, 1, 1, 3∣σ1​+2σ2​∣=3,1,1,3, with mean 2. Hence R^S=B2⋅2=B\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S = \tfrac{B}{2}\cdot 2 = BR^S​=2B​⋅2=B, while the bound of the proposition is B21+4≈1.118 B\tfrac{B}{2}\sqrt{1 + 4} \approx 1.118\,B2B​1+4​≈1.118B: close, but not equal, as Jensen’s inequality predicts. The check by enumeration of the sign vectors:

signs = np.array(list(product([-1, 1], repeat=2)))          # the four sign vectors
x_pts = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
B_rad = 1.0
exact = B_rad / 2 * np.mean(np.abs(signs @ x_pts))
bound = B_rad / 2 * np.sqrt(np.sum(x_pts ** 2))
print(f"empirical Rademacher complexity (B=1): {exact:.4f} | bound of Proposition 3.6: {bound:.4f}")
empirical Rademacher complexity (B=1): 1.0000 | bound of Proposition 3.6: 1.1180

3.8.3 Measured on a real data set¶

Let us measure R^S(F1)\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\mathcal{F}_1)R^S​(F1​) for the 30 standardized features of the Breast Cancer data, for samples of increasing size drawn from the 569 patients, by Monte Carlo: for each sample we draw 2000 random sign vectors and average ∥∑iσixi∥2/n\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i\mathbf{x}_i\rVert_2/n∥∑i​σi​xi​∥2​/n, which is the exact value by Proposition 3.6. We compare it with the two bounds of the proposition: the sharper one that uses the actual norms of the sample points, ∑i∥xi∥2/n\sqrt{\sum_i\lVert\mathbf{x}_i\rVert^2}/n∑i​∥xi​∥2​/n, and the cruder one that uses only the largest norm RRR.

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X_std = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_bc)                         # the 569 x 30 Breast Cancer matrix, standardized
R_max = np.linalg.norm(X_std, axis=1).max()
print(f"largest norm of a data point: R = {R_max:.2f} (the typical norm is about {np.sqrt(30):.2f})")

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
rows = []
for n in [25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 569]:
    Xs = X_std[rng.choice(N_BC, size=n, replace=False)]
    sigma = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(2000, n))
    rademacher_mc = np.linalg.norm(sigma @ Xs, axis=1).mean() / n   # B = 1
    rows.append({"n": n, "Rademacher complexity (Monte Carlo)": rademacher_mc,
                 "bound with the actual norms": np.sqrt((Xs ** 2).sum()) / n, "bound R/sqrt(n)": R_max / np.sqrt(n)})
rademacher_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(rademacher_table.round(4).to_string(index=False))
largest norm of a data point: R = 20.55 (the typical norm is about 5.48)

def figure_3_9():
    from matplotlib.ticker import NullFormatter, ScalarFormatter

    r = rademacher_table
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
    ax.plot(r["n"], r["Rademacher complexity (Monte Carlo)"], color="black", marker="o", linewidth=2.2, label="Monte Carlo value")
    ax.plot(r["n"], r["bound with the actual norms"], color=BLUE, marker="s", linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label=r"bound $\sqrt{\sum_i\|x_i\|^2}\,/\,n$")
    ax.plot(r["n"], r["bound R/sqrt(n)"], color=VERMILION, marker="^", linestyle=":", linewidth=2, label=r"bound $R/\sqrt{n}$ ($R$ = largest norm)")
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="sample size $n$", ylabel=r"$\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S$ of $\{\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}: \|\mathbf{w}\|\leq 1\}$",

The Monte Carlo value is 3% to 7% below the first bound, so Jensen’s inequality costs very little here, and it follows the 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​ slope. The cruder bound R/nR/\sqrt{n}R/n​ is about four times larger than the truth: it uses the largest norm in the data (20.5, an outlier among patients), while the typical norm is about 5.5. This is a useful lesson: the data-dependent version of a bound, which uses the actual sample, is much tighter than the version that uses worst-case quantities.

3.8.4 Margins: why large-margin classifiers generalize¶

For classification we want the 0–1 loss, which is not Lipschitz, so the contraction lemma does not apply to it directly. The trick is to bound it by a Lipschitz function of the margin y f(x)y\,f(\mathbf{x})yf(x) of a prediction (positive when the prediction is correct, and large when it is confidently correct; labels are y∈{−1,+1}y \in \{-1, +1\}y∈{−1,+1} here). Fix a margin level γ>0\gamma > 0γ>0 and define the ramp loss φγ(z)=min⁡{1,max⁡{0,1−z/γ}}\varphi_\gamma(z) = \min\{1, \max\{0, 1 - z/\gamma\}\}φγ​(z)=min{1,max{0,1−z/γ}}: it equals 1 for z≤0z \le 0z≤0, decreases linearly to 0 at z=γz = \gammaz=γ, and is 1γ\tfrac1\gammaγ1​-Lipschitz. It sits between the two quantities that we care about:

I[z≤0] ≤ φγ(z) ≤ I[z<γ].\mathbb{I}[z \le 0] \ \le\ \varphi_\gamma(z) \ \le\ \mathbb{I}[z < \gamma].I[z≤0] ≤ φγ​(z) ≤ I[z<γ].
(45)

The left side says that the ramp loss bounds the 0–1 loss (the loss we want to control); the right side says that its empirical average is at most the fraction of training points with margin below γ\gammaγ. Applying Theorem 3.5 to the class {φγ(yf(x))}\{\varphi_\gamma(y f(\mathbf{x}))\}{φγ​(yf(x))} and the contraction lemma (the labels only flip the signs of the Rademacher variables, which does not change their distribution), we obtain:

Theorem 3.7 (margin bound for norm-bounded linear classifiers). Let ∥x∥2≤R\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_2 \le R∥x∥2​≤R almost surely and γ>0\gamma > 0γ>0. With probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, all w\mathbf{w}w with ∥w∥2≤B\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le B∥w∥2​≤B satisfy

P(y w⊤x≤0) ≤ 1n #{i:yi w⊤xi<γ}+2BRγn+ln⁡(1/δ)2n.\mathbb{P}\big(y\,\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} \le 0\big) \ \le\ \frac{1}{n}\,\#\big\{i : y_i\,\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i < \gamma\big\} + \frac{2BR}{\gamma\sqrt{n}} + \sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}} .P(yw⊤x≤0) ≤ n1​#{i:yi​w⊤xi​<γ}+γn​2BR​+2nln(1/δ)​​.
(46)

Read the three terms. The first is the fraction of training points that are misclassified or classified with a margin smaller than γ\gammaγ. The second is the capacity of the class and depends on BR/γBR/\gammaBR/γ, the radius of the weights times the radius of the data divided by the margin; it does not depend on ddd. The third is the confidence term. If a classifier has no training points below margin γ\gammaγ with a small ∥w∥\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∥w∥, the bound is small; to get a small second term we want a small norm for a given margin. This is exactly what a support vector machine optimizes (Chapter 8: maximize the margin, equivalently minimize ∥w∥\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∥w∥ with margin fixed at 1), and, in a softer way, what ridge regression and weight decay do (Chapter 6: penalize ∥w∥2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2∥w∥2). The same bound is what makes kernel methods work in infinite dimensions (Chapter 9).

Key idea

Three ways of measuring the capacity of a class, one message. For a finite class the capacity is ln⁡∣H∣\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvertln∣H∣ (Section 3.6). For an infinite class it is the VC dimension, through dln⁡nd\ln ndlnn (Section 3.7), or the Rademacher complexity, which measures how well the class fits random signs on the data (this section). In all three, the generalization gap shrinks like capacity/n\sqrt{\text{capacity}/n}capacity/n​: the training set must be large compared with the capacity of the model. They differ in what capacity depends on: the number of functions, the combinatorial richness of the class, or, for Rademacher, the norm of the weights and the geometry of the data. Regularization, margins and early stopping do not change the number of parameters, but they shrink the effective class, and that is why they work.

3.9 No free lunch: why learning needs assumptions¶

All the bounds of this chapter had the same structure: the generalization gap is controlled by a capacity of the class H\mathcal{H}H that we fixed in advance. It is natural to ask whether there is a learning algorithm that needs no such restriction, a universal learner that is good on every problem. The answer is a clear no, and the proof is short enough to give in full.

Theorem 3.8 (No Free Lunch, finite version). Let the input domain be a finite set X\mathcal{X}X with NNN points, and suppose the labels are given by an arbitrary target function t:X→{0,1}t: \mathcal{X} \to \{0, 1\}t:X→{0,1} (all 2N2^N2N functions are possible). A learning algorithm sees the labels t(x)t(\mathbf{x})t(x) on n<Nn < Nn<N training points and must predict the labels of the other N−nN - nN−n points. Then, for every algorithm, the accuracy on the unseen points, averaged over all 2N2^N2N targets, is exactly 12\tfrac1221​.

Proof. Fix the training points. Group the 2N2^N2N targets according to the labels they give to these nnn points: there are 2n2^n2n groups, each containing the 2N−n2^{N-n}2N−n targets that agree on the training points and take all possible values on the other N−nN - nN−n points. All the targets of one group give the algorithm the same training data, so the algorithm makes the same predictions for all of them. Take an unseen point x\mathbf{x}x: in each group, exactly half of the targets give it the label 1 and half the label 0, so whatever the algorithm predicts for x\mathbf{x}x, it is right for exactly half of the group. Hence the average accuracy on every unseen point, and therefore on all of them, is 12\tfrac1221​. □\square□

Wolpert (1996) proved the general version for noisy targets and arbitrary loss functions, and Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David give a probabilistic version (for any algorithm and any n<∣X∣/2n < \lvert\mathcal{X}\rvert/2n<∣X∣/2 there is a distribution on which the algorithm fails with constant probability). We can watch the theorem at work by enumerating all the 28=2562^8 = 25628=256 Boolean functions of three bits, training four learners on four of the eight points and testing them on the other four.

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

points = np.array(list(product([0, 1], repeat=3)))                   # the 8 points of the domain {0,1}^3
train_idx, test_idx = np.array([0, 3, 5, 6]), np.array([1, 2, 4, 7])
all_targets = np.array(list(product([0, 1], repeat=8)))              # every possible labeling of the 8 points: 256 functions


def majority(X_tr, y_tr, X_te):
    return np.full(len(X_te), int(y_tr.mean() > 0.5))


def one_nn(X_tr, y_tr, X_te):
    return KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=1).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te) if len(set(y_tr)) > 1 else np.full(len(X_te), y_tr[0])


def stump(X_tr, y_tr, X_te):
    return DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te)


def anti_stump(X_tr, y_tr, X_te):
    return 1 - stump(X_tr, y_tr, X_te)


def mean_accuracy(learner, targets):
    return np.mean([np.mean(learner(points[train_idx], t[train_idx], points[test_idx]) == t[test_idx]) for t in targets])


# A tiny "structured world": the six targets that copy one bit or its opposite
dictators = np.array([points[:, j] for j in range(3)] + [1 - points[:, j] for j in range(3)])
learners = {"majority vote": majority, "1-nearest neighbor": one_nn, "decision stump": stump, "anti-stump (opposite of the stump)": anti_stump}
nfl_table = pd.DataFrame({"all 256 targets": {k: mean_accuracy(f, all_targets) for k, f in learners.items()},
                          "6 'copy one bit' targets": {k: mean_accuracy(f, dictators) for k, f in learners.items()}})
nfl_table.round(4)
Loading...

The first column is Theorem 3.8: every learner, even the absurd “anti-stump”, has an average accuracy of exactly 0.5 over the 256 possible targets. Learning is impossible on average over all worlds. The second column shows what happens when the world is not arbitrary. If we know that the target simply copies one bit or its opposite, a stump (which can express exactly that) gets every unseen point right, 1-nearest neighbor does better than chance (0.67) and the anti-stump gets every one wrong. The learner that does well is not “better” in any absolute sense: its assumptions fit the world.

Key idea

Learning is possible only because we make assumptions about how the world is: the inductive bias of a method. The theorem does not say that learning is impossible; it says that it is impossible without assumptions, and that every method embodies some. The real world is far from “all functions equally likely”: nearby inputs tend to have similar labels, few features matter, relationships are smooth or compositional. Choosing a model family is choosing which of these assumptions to bet on. The rest of the book can be read as a catalog of inductive biases:

MethodAssumption about the worldChapter
kkk-nearest neighborssimilar inputs have similar labels4
linear and logistic modelsthe label depends on a linear combination of the features6
ridge, Lassothe weights are small, or only a few are non-zero6, 10
support vector machines, kernelsthe classes are separated by a large margin in some feature space8, 9
decision trees and ensemblesthe label depends on a few features through simple threshold rules11
convolutional networkspatterns are local and the same everywhere in the image16, 17
recurrent networks, transformersthe order of the elements, and their dependencies, matter18, 19

3.10 Theory meets practice¶

3.10.1 The generalization gap on a real data set¶

How do the bounds fare on real data? We train a logistic regression on the Breast Cancer data with training sets of increasing size, repeating each size 300 times with random splits, and measure the generalization gap: the test error minus the training error. The test set is whatever is left (569 minus nnn patients), so it is large for small nnn. (The pipeline standardizes the features, as in Chapter 1; we use the default regularization, C=1.)

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
rows = []
for n in [30, 60, 120, 240, 455]:
    train_err, test_err = [], []
    for _ in range(300):
        perm = rng.permutation(N_BC)
        tr, te = perm[:n], perm[n:]
        model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)).fit(X_bc[tr], y_bc[tr])
        train_err.append(np.mean(model.predict(X_bc[tr]) != y_bc[tr]))
        test_err.append(np.mean(model.predict(X_bc[te]) != y_bc[te]))
    rows.append({"n": n, "training error": np.mean(train_err), "test error": np.mean(test_err)})
gap_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
gap_table["mean gap"] = gap_table["test error"] - gap_table["training error"]
gap_table["VC term (d_VC = 31)"] = vc_term(gap_table["n"], 31)
slope = np.polyfit(np.log(gap_table["n"]), np.log(gap_table["mean gap"]), 1)[0]
print(gap_table.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nslope of log(gap) against log(n): {slope:.2f}   (1/sqrt(n) would give -0.50)")

120          0.0095      0.0333    0.0238               2.5668
240          0.0107      0.0278    0.0172               2.0026
455          0.0115      0.0228    0.0113               1.5697

slope of log(gap) against log(n): -0.58   (1/sqrt(n) would give -0.50)

# Figure 3.10 — the gap on real data against the VC term, and the half-width of the test-set interval
def figure_3_10():
    g = gap_table
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.2, 4.4))

    ax = axes[0]
    ax.plot(g["n"], g["VC term (d_VC = 31)"], color=BLUE, marker="s", linestyle="--", linewidth=2, label="VC bound term, $d_{VC}$ = 31")
    ax.plot(g["n"], g["mean gap"], color=VERMILION, marker="o", linewidth=2, label="measured gap (logistic regression)")
    ax.plot(g["n"], g["mean gap"].iloc[0] * np.sqrt(g["n"].iloc[0] / g["n"]), color="gray", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.5,
            label=r"$\propto 1/\sqrt{n}$, through the first point")
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xticks(list(g["n"])); ax.set_xticklabels(list(g["n"])); ax.minorticks_off()
    ax.set(xlabel="training-set size $n$", ylabel="generalization gap", title="(a) the bound is loose, the trend is right")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, loc="center right")

    ax = axes[1]
    m = np.logspace(1.2, 4.2, 200)
    ax.plot(m, np.sqrt(np.log(2 / 0.05) / (2 * m)), color=GREEN, linewidth=2.2)
    for m_mark, label, dy in [(114, "114 test patients: $\\pm$0.127", 1.15), (4612, "4612 test examples: $\\pm$0.02", 1.45)]:
        eps_mark = np.sqrt(np.log(2 / 0.05) / (2 * m_mark))
        ax.plot(m_mark, eps_mark, marker="o", color="black", markersize=7)
        ax.annotate(label, (m_mark, eps_mark), xytext=(m_mark * 1.25, eps_mark * dy), fontsize=9.5)
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set(xlabel="size $m$ of the test set", ylabel="half-width of the 95% Hoeffding interval",
           title="(b) how precise is a test error?")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_3_10()

The gap of the logistic regression falls from 5.7 percentage points at n=30n = 30n=30 to 1.1 at n=455n = 455n=455: a decrease with a log-log slope of -0.58, close to the −12-\tfrac12−21​ of 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​ (the dotted line). The VC term, in contrast, is between 1.6 and 3.9 over the same range: it is vacuous and 70 to 140 times larger than the real gap. Both facts are what Section 3.7 predicted: the bound is worst-case over all distributions and all algorithms, and ours is neither; but it correctly says that the gap shrinks as the sample grows and that the speed is of the order of 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​ (with a logarithmic factor). Use the theory for the shape (what matters and how it scales), not for the numbers. The numbers come from experiments with held-out data, as in the next subsection.

3.10.2 The one bound you will use every day: sizing a test set¶

There is one situation in which Hoeffding’s inequality applies without a union bound and without loss: the evaluation of one function on fresh data. If a function fff was chosen without looking at the test set TTT of mmm examples (which are i.i.d. from D\mathcal{D}D and independent of the training set), then fff is “fixed in advance” with respect to TTT, and with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ

∣R^T(f)−R(f)∣≤ln⁡(2/δ)2m.\big\lvert \hat{R}_T(f) - R(f)\big\rvert \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta)}{2m}}.∣∣​R^T​(f)−R(f)∣∣​≤2mln(2/δ)​​.
(47)

So a test set is the right tool, and the formula tells how big it must be. For an error rate known to within ±0.02\pm 0.02±0.02 with 95% confidence, m≥ln⁡(40)/(2⋅0.022)=4611.1m \ge \ln(40)/(2 \cdot 0.02^2) = 4611.1m≥ln(40)/(2⋅0.022)=4611.1, that is 4612 examples; for ±0.01\pm 0.01±0.01 it is four times as many. Panel (b) of Figure 3.10 shows the half-width as a function of mmm. A data set of 569 patients with a test set of 114 (20%) gives a half-width of 0.127: the guarantee for that test set is weak, which is a consequence of how little data a test set of 114 contains, not of the method.

# One 80/20 split of the Breast Cancer data; the model is chosen and fitted on the training part only
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
perm = rng.permutation(N_BC)
tr, te = perm[:455], perm[455:]
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)).fit(X_bc[tr], y_bc[tr])
m_test = len(te)
k_err = int(np.sum(model.predict(X_bc[te]) != y_bc[te]))
half = np.sqrt(np.log(2 / 0.05) / (2 * m_test))
wilson = stats.binomtest(k_err, m_test).proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95, method="wilson")
exact_ci = stats.binomtest(k_err, m_test).proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95, method="exact")
print(f"test set of {m_test} patients: {k_err} errors, test error {k_err / m_test:.3f}")
print(f"Hoeffding 95% interval for the true risk   : [{max(0, k_err / m_test - half):.3f}, {k_err / m_test + half:.3f}]  (half-width {half:.3f})")
print(f"Wilson 95% interval                        : [{wilson.low:.3f}, {wilson.high:.3f}]")
print(f"Clopper-Pearson (exact) 95% interval       : [{exact_ci.low:.3f}, {exact_ci.high:.3f}]")
for k_models in (1, 10, 100):
    print(f"best of {k_models:>3} models compared on this test set: half-width {np.sqrt(np.log(2 * k_models / 0.05) / (2 * m_test)):.3f}")
test set of 114 patients: 1 errors, test error 0.009
Hoeffding 95% interval for the true risk   : [0.000, 0.136]  (half-width 0.127)
Wilson 95% interval                        : [0.002, 0.048]
Clopper-Pearson (exact) 95% interval       : [0.000, 0.048]
best of   1 models compared on this test set: half-width 0.127
best of  10 models compared on this test set: half-width 0.162
best of 100 models compared on this test set: half-width 0.191

The test error of this split is 0.9% (one mistake in 114 patients). The Hoeffding interval is wide: it reaches 0.136, because its half-width ±0.127\pm 0.127±0.127 does not depend on how small the error is. The other two intervals, which exploit the fact that the error rate is small (a Bernoulli variable with small ppp has a small variance, which Hoeffding ignores), are about three times narrower (both end at 0.048). They are the intervals to report in practice; Exercise 3.10 compares their coverage. The last lines of the output show what happens if a test set is used to choose among kkk models: the guarantee degrades only like ln⁡k\ln klnk (that is the union bound of Section 3.6), but, more importantly, the winner’s curse of Section 3.4 returns. This is why we need three sets in practice: a training set to fit, a validation set to choose, a test set to report once (Chapter 5).

3.10.3 What the theory does not explain¶

The theory of this chapter is a foundation, not the end of the story, and it is honest to say where it stops.

  • The bounds are loose by one to two orders of magnitude on real problems, as we have just measured. Tighter ones exist for particular classes and distributions (PAC-Bayes bounds, stability-based bounds), and are an active area of research.

  • Modern deep networks have far more parameters than training examples, their VC dimension is enormous, and they can fit random labels perfectly (Zhang et al., 2017); yet they generalize well on real data. The classical capacity measures of this chapter do not explain this, and the answer involves the dynamics of the optimizer and the structure of real data (Chapter 15).

  • The i.i.d. assumption (Section 3.2.1) fails whenever the data are collected over time, or the application differs from the training population; handling distribution shift requires different tools.

  • The chapter studied how large the gap can be. It did not say how to find a function with a small empirical risk (optimization, Chapter 7), nor how to choose among the models of different complexity (model selection, Chapter 5).

3.11 Summary¶

  • Setting. Data are i.i.d. draws from an unknown distribution D\mathcal{D}D. The goal is a small expected risk R(f)=E[ℓ(y,f(x))]R(f) = \mathbb{E}[\ell(y, f(\mathbf{x}))]R(f)=E[ℓ(y,f(x))]; what we can compute is the empirical risk R^S(f)\hat{R}_S(f)R^S​(f). The Bayes predictor (the conditional mean for the squared loss, the most probable class for the 0–1 loss) has the smallest possible risk R∗R^\astR∗, which is positive when the labels are noisy.

  • ERM and its error. Empirical risk minimization over a class H\mathcal{H}H has excess risk = estimation error (random, shrinks with nnn, grows with the richness of H\mathcal{H}H) + approximation error (a property of H\mathcal{H}H, independent of nnn). The best complexity grows with nnn; the training error always prefers the richer class and cannot choose it.

  • Optimism. E[R^S(f^S)]≤R(fH)≤E[R(f^S)]\mathbb{E}[\hat{R}_S(\hat f_S)] \le R(f_{\mathcal{H}}) \le \mathbb{E}[R(\hat f_S)]E[R^S​(f^​S​)]≤R(fH​)≤E[R(f^​S​)]. Picking the best of many candidates inflates the apparent performance by about ln⁡m/(2n)\sqrt{\ln m/(2n)}lnm/(2n)​.

  • Concentration. Markov →\to→ Chebyshev (polynomial decay) →\to→ Chernoff →\to→ Hoeffding: for nnn i.i.d. variables in [0,1][0, 1][0,1], P(∣Xˉn−μ∣≥ε)≤2e−2nε2\mathbb{P}(\lvert\bar X_n - \mu\rvert \ge \varepsilon) \le 2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}P(∣Xˉn​−μ∣≥ε)≤2e−2nε2. A fixed function has ∣R^S−R∣≤ln⁡(2/δ)/(2n)\lvert\hat{R}_S - R\rvert \le \sqrt{\ln(2/\delta)/(2n)}∣R^S​−R∣≤ln(2/δ)/(2n)​ with probability 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ.

  • Finite classes. The union bound gives ∣R−R^S∣≤(ln⁡∣H∣+ln⁡(2/δ))/(2n)\lvert R - \hat{R}_S\rvert \le \sqrt{(\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvert + \ln(2/\delta))/(2n)}∣R−R^S​∣≤(ln∣H∣+ln(2/δ))/(2n)​ for all f∈Hf \in \mathcal{H}f∈H at once, so the estimation error of ERM is at most twice that. The class enters only through ln⁡∣H∣\ln\lvert\mathcal{H}\rvertln∣H∣.

  • Infinite classes. The VC dimension is the size of the largest shattered set (d+1d + 1d+1 for linear classifiers in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd; Cover’s counting formula). By Sauer–Shelah the growth function is polynomial after dVCd_{\mathrm{VC}}dVC​, and the gap is at most (8/n)(dln⁡(2en/d)+ln⁡(4/δ))\sqrt{(8/n)(d\ln(2en/d) + \ln(4/\delta))}(8/n)(dln(2en/d)+ln(4/δ))​. Parameters are not capacity (sin⁡(ωx)\sin(\omega x)sin(ωx) has one parameter and infinite VC dimension). A linear classifier fits random labels once d≳n/2d \gtrsim n/2d≳n/2.

  • Rademacher complexity measures how well a class fits random signs on the data. For ∥w∥2≤B\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_2 \le B∥w∥2​≤B and ∥x∥2≤R\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert_2 \le R∥x∥2​≤R it is at most BR/nBR/\sqrt{n}BR/n​, independent of the dimension. The margin bound has the capacity term 2BR/(γn)2BR/(\gamma\sqrt{n})2BR/(γn​): small norm and large margin control generalization, which is the reason for regularization, SVMs and kernels.

  • No Free Lunch. Averaged over all possible targets every learner has accuracy 12\tfrac1221​ on unseen data. Learning needs inductive biases, and choosing a model family is choosing one.

  • In practice. The bounds are loose by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude, but they predict the shape (1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​, capacity\sqrt{\text{capacity}}capacity​). The practical bound is Hoeffding’s for a test set: ±ln⁡(2/δ)/(2m)\pm\sqrt{\ln(2/\delta)/(2m)}±ln(2/δ)/(2m)​, so 4612 test examples for ±0.02\pm 0.02±0.02 at 95% confidence.

Data sources¶

  • Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic): W. N. Street, W. H. Wolberg and O. L. Mangasarian, “Nuclear feature extraction for breast tumor diagnosis”, IS&T/SPIE 1993 International Symposium on Electronic Imaging: Science and Technology, volume 1905, 861–870 (1993). Bundled with scikit-learn. In Section 3.6.1 the 569 patients are used as the population of a bootstrap world, and in Sections 3.8 and 3.10 as an ordinary data set.

  • The simulated world of Sections 3.2 to 3.4 (two Gaussian classes in the plane) and the coin-flip experiments of Sections 3.4, 3.5 and 3.7 are simulations: they are used because the theory needs a distribution that is known exactly.

Further reading¶

  • S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2014. The closest book to this chapter, with all the proofs we omitted (Sauer–Shelah, VC, Rademacher, No Free Lunch).

  • M. Mohri, A. Rostamizadeh and A. Talwalkar, Foundations of Machine Learning, 2nd ed., MIT Press, 2018. Rademacher complexity and margin bounds in full detail (Chapters 3 and 5).

  • Y. S. Abu-Mostafa, M. Magdon-Ismail and H.-T. Lin, Learning From Data, AMLBook, 2012. A very readable account of the VC dimension and of the form of the bound of Theorem 3.4.

  • T. Hastie, R. Tibshirani and J. Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Springer, 2009. Chapter 7 (model assessment and selection), with the statistician’s view of optimism and of the bias–variance trade-off.

  • V. N. Vapnik, Statistical Learning Theory, Wiley, 1998; V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis, “On the uniform convergence of relative frequencies of events to their probabilities”, Theory of Probability and Its Applications 16(2), 264–280 (1971). The original sources of the VC theory.

  • S. Boucheron, G. Lugosi and P. Massart, Concentration Inequalities: A Nonasymptotic Theory of Independence, Oxford University Press, 2013. For Hoeffding, Bernstein and the rest of the family.

  • W. Hoeffding, “Probability inequalities for sums of bounded random variables”, Journal of the American Statistical Association 58(301), 13–30 (1963).

  • T. M. Cover, “Geometrical and statistical properties of systems of linear inequalities with applications in pattern recognition”, IEEE Transactions on Electronic Computers EC-14(3), 326–334 (1965).

  • P. L. Bartlett and S. Mendelson, “Rademacher and Gaussian complexities: risk bounds and structural results”, Journal of Machine Learning Research 3, 463–482 (2002).

  • L. G. Valiant, “A theory of the learnable”, Communications of the ACM 27(11), 1134–1142 (1984). The paper that started the PAC (probably approximately correct) framework.

  • D. H. Wolpert, “The lack of a priori distinctions between learning algorithms”, Neural Computation 8(7), 1341–1390 (1996).

  • C. Zhang, S. Bengio, M. Hardt, B. Recht and O. Vinyals, “Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization”, International Conference on Learning Representations (2017).

(a) Prove that for the squared loss E[(y−f(x))2]=E[(y−η(x))2]+E[(η(x)−f(x))2]\mathbb{E}\big[(y - f(\mathbf{x}))^2\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[(y - \eta(\mathbf{x}))^2\big] + \mathbb{E}\big[(\eta(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}))^2\big]E[(y−f(x))2]=E[(y−η(x))2]+E[(η(x)−f(x))2], with η(x)=E[y∣x]\eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}]η(x)=E[y∣x]. Exercise 3.3 ★★ — Sizing a test set. You want to estimate the error rate of a classifier on fresh data to within ±0.03\pm 0.03±0.03 with 95% confidence. (a) How many test examples does Hoeffding’s inequality require? (b) How many does Chebyshev’s inequality require in the worst case? (c) If you know that the true error rate is around 0.05, Chebyshev with the actual variance p(1−p)p(1 - p)p(1−p) asks for fewer examples than Hoeffding. Compute the number and explain why a bound that is worse in general can win here. (d) With only 1000 test examples, what is the half-width of the Hoeffding interval?

Exercise 3.7 ★★ — Approximation and estimation in regression. Let x∼U[0,1]x \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1]x∼U[0,1] and y=sin⁡(2πx)+εy = \sin(2\pi x) + \varepsilony=sin(2πx)+ε with ε∼N(0,0.32)\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.3^2)ε∼N(0,0.32), so that the Bayes risk for the squared loss is σ2=0.09\sigma^2 = 0.09σ2=0.09. The hypothesis class Hm\mathcal{H}_mHm​ is the set of polynomials of degree at most mmm, fitted by least squares (np.polyfit). (a) For m∈{1,3,6}m \in \{1, 3, 6\}m∈{1,3,6} estimate the risk of fHmf_{\mathcal{H}_m}fHm​​ (the best polynomial; fit it on 105 points) and hence the approximation error R(fHm)−R∗R(f_{\mathcal{H}_m}) - R^\astR(fHm​​)−R∗. What comes next¶

With this chapter Part I is complete: we know what a learning problem is (Chapter 1), the tools to work with data (Chapter 2), and why learning from a sample is possible and what it costs (Chapter 3). From Chapter 4 on we study learning methods one at a time. We begin with the simplest one, kkk-nearest neighbors, which you already implemented in Chapter 2, and we use it to see the trade-off of Section 3.3 in its classical form for the squared loss: the bias–variance decomposition, and why the “right” kkk depends on the amount of data. Chapter 5 turns the lessons of Sections 3.4 and 3.10 into practice: validation sets, cross-validation, and the metrics (precision, recall, ROC curves) with which classifiers are compared. In Chapter 6 the norm bounds of Section 3.8 will appear as ridge regression and regularized logistic regression, and Chapters 8 and 9 build on the margin bound of Theorem 3.7 to derive support vector machines and kernel methods.
